It was built under the direction of General Mikhail Annenkov.

q.q: Which desert did the Trans-Caspian Railway cross?

samarkand.name: Samarkand
samarkand.t: The blue-domed crossroads of the Silk Road
samarkand.s: Samarkand is more than 2,500 years old and was for centuries the great meeting point of the Silk Road. Under Timur and his descendants in the 14th and 15th centuries it was filled with turquoise domes and tiled madrasas, and its Registan square is still one of the grandest in the Islamic world. From above, look for the city spread across the green Zeravshan valley, with mountains rising to the south.
samarkand.w: Look for a large city in the green, irrigated Zeravshan valley, with mountain ridges to the south and desert beyond.
f: The ruler Ulugh Beg built an observatory here in the 1420s and catalogued about a thousand stars.
Samarkand paper was famous across the Islamic world from the 8th century.
The city became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2001.

q.q: Which ruler built an observatory in Samarkand?

bukhara.name: Bukhara
bukhara.t: A holy city of scholars, domes and bazaars
bukhara.s: In an oasis at the end of the Zeravshan river lies Bukhara, one of the best-preserved medieval cities of Central Asia. In the 9th and 10th centuries it was the capital of the Samanids and a centre of Persian poetry and science. Its old centre still has covered bazaars, madrasas and a 12th-century minaret. From above, look for a green oasis surrounded by desert, west of Samarkand.
bukhara.w: Look for a green irrigated oasis ringed by desert, about 220 km west of Samarkand.
f: The physician and philosopher Avicenna was born near Bukhara in 980.
The Kalyan Minaret, built in 1127, rises about 46 m above the old town.
The Samanid Mausoleum, from the 10th century, is a masterpiece of decorative brickwork.

q.q: Which great physician was born near Bukhara?

khiva.name: Khiva
khiva.t: A walled desert town like a museum under open sky
khiva.s: On the edge of the Karakum desert, in the delta oasis of the Amu Darya, stands Khiva. Its inner town, Itchan Kala, is enclosed by mud-brick walls and crammed with minarets, madrasas and palaces, mostly from the 18th and 19th centuries. It was the last stop before caravans crossed the desert to Persia. From above, look for the green irrigated oasis sharp against sand on every side.
khiva.w: Look for a large green irrigated oasis on the Amu Darya, with bare desert pressing in on all sides.
f: Itchan Kala became Uzbekistan's first UNESCO World Heritage site in 1990.
The Kalta Minor minaret was left unfinished and stands short and wide, covered in turquoise tiles.
The mathematician al-Khwarizmi, whose name gave us the word 'algorithm', came from this region.

q.q: Which word comes from the name of Khwarazm's mathematician?

merv.name: Merv
merv.t: Once one of the largest cities in the world
merv.s: In the delta of the Murghab river, in the Karakum desert, lie the ruins of Merv. For 2,000 years a succession of walled cities rose side by side here, each built next to the last. In the 12th century, as capital of the Seljuk sultans, it was among the largest cities on Earth. From above, look for the green oasis of Mary amid the desert; the ruins lie just east of the town.
merv.w: Look for the green delta oasis of the Murghab river in the Karakum; the ruins lie just east of the city of Mary.
f: The mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar, from the 12th century, still has its great brick dome.
Its oldest walled city, Erk Kala, dates to the Achaemenid Persian era.
Ancient Merv became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1999.

q.q: In which river's delta did Merv grow?

ani.name: Ani
ani.t: The medieval city of a thousand and one churches
ani.s: On a triangle of plateau above a river gorge stand the ruins of Ani, capital of a medieval Armenian kingdom. In the 11th century it was one of the great cities of its age, its skyline crowded with churches. Many still stand, roofless, on the open grassland. From above, look for the high plateau and the deep gorge that today marks the border between Turkey and Armenia.
ani.w: Look for a high green-brown plateau cut by a deep river gorge, east of the town of Kars.
f: Ani was nicknamed 'the city of 1,001 churches'.
Its cathedral, finished around 1001, uses pointed arches long before Gothic Europe.
Ani became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2016.

q.q: What was Ani's nickname?

mtskheta.name: Mtskheta
mtskheta.t: Georgia's ancient capital where two rivers meet
mtskheta.s: Just north of Tbilisi, where the Aragvi flows into the Kura, lies Mtskheta, the ancient capital of the Georgian kingdom of Iberia. Here Georgia adopted Christianity in the 4th century, one of the first countries to do so. A small 6th-century monastery, Jvari, watches over the confluence from a hilltop. From above, look for the two rivers meeting in a green valley, often in two different colours.
mtskheta.w: Look for two rivers joining in a narrow green valley about 20 km north of Tbilisi.
f: Svetitskhoveli Cathedral in Mtskheta was built in the 11th century on an older church site.
Jvari Monastery gave its name to a whole style of Georgian church architecture.
Mtskheta's churches became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1994.

q.q: Which two rivers meet at Mtskheta?

derbent.name: Derbent
derbent.t: The Gate of Gates between mountains and sea
derbent.s: Here the Caucasus mountains come within a few kilometres of the Caspian Sea, leaving a narrow pass along the coast. In the 6th century Persian kings built two parallel stone walls from the mountain fortress down into the sea to control it. Arab geographers called it the Gate of Gates. From above, the reason is obvious: a thin coastal strip squeezed between blue water and steep ridges.
derbent.w: Look for a narrow coastal plain squeezed between the Caspian Sea and the steep foothills of the Caucasus.
f: Derbent is often called the oldest city in Russia.
Its walls once ran out into the sea, forming a guarded harbour.
The citadel and old city became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2003.

q.q: Which sea do Derbent's walls run down to?

baikonur.name: Baikonur, launch site of the first human spaceflight
baikonur.t: Where the first human left for space
baikonur.s: On the flat steppe of Kazakhstan, near the Syr Darya river, lies the world's first spaceport. The first artificial satellite, Sputnik, was launched from here in 1957. On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin lifted off from the same pad to become the first human in space. From above, look for the ribbon of the Syr Darya across the dry steppe, and the town of Baikonur beside it.
baikonur.w: Look for the thin green ribbon of the Syr Darya crossing flat, dry steppe, with a town and scattered launch complexes north of it.
f: Gagarin's flight lasted 108 minutes and made one orbit of the Earth.
His launch pad, known as Gagarin's Start, stayed in use for more than 60 years.
The cosmodrome is leased by Russia from Kazakhstan.

q.q: How long did Gagarin's first spaceflight last?

arkaim.name: Arkaim
arkaim.t: A ring-shaped Bronze Age town in the Ural steppe
arkaim.s: On the open steppe east of the southern Urals lie the remains of Arkaim, a fortified settlement built around 4,000 years ago as two rings of walls with houses set against them. It belongs to the Sintashta culture, known for some of the world's earliest spoked-wheel chariots. The rings are too faint to see from cruise, but the rolling grassland around them has changed little since.
arkaim.w: Look for open, rolling steppe with river valleys and few trees, south of Chelyabinsk and east of the Ural ridges.
f: Arkaim was found in 1987 by archaeologists surveying land for a planned reservoir.
The discovery led to the reservoir plan being dropped and the land becoming a reserve.
The settlement was about 150 m across.

q.q: What nearly flooded Arkaim soon after it was found?

khorezm.name: Khwarazm
khorezm.t: An oasis kingdom on the Amu Darya delta
khorezm.s: Where the Amu Darya fans out before the Aral Sea, irrigation created a green island between two deserts: Khwarazm, home to kingdoms for 2,500 years. Dozens of ancient mud-brick fortresses still stand on the desert edge, and its old capital, Konye-Urgench, keeps a soaring minaret. From cruise the oasis is one of the region's clearest sights: a big patch of green and water in beige desert.
khorezm.w: A large green patchwork of irrigated fields and canals on the lower Amu Darya, between the Karakum and Kyzylkum deserts.
f: The scholar al-Biruni, born here in 973, calculated the Earth's radius with remarkable accuracy.
The Kutlug Timur minaret in Konye-Urgench is about 60 m tall.
The fortresses of ancient Khwarazm are among the oldest in Central Asia.

q.q: Which scholar born in Khwarazm measured the Earth's radius?

bactria.name: Bactria
bactria.t: Where Greek, Persian and Indian worlds met
bactria.s: Between the Hindu Kush and the Amu Darya lay Bactria, a rich land of oasis cities. It was a Persian province, then a Greek kingdom founded by Alexander's successors, then the heart of the Kushan empire, which carried Buddhism north along the Silk Road. Its chief city, Balkh, was called the mother of cities. From above, look for the Amu Darya's green valley with the Hindu Kush to the south.
bactria.w: Look for the green valley of the Amu Darya, with the high, often snowy Hindu Kush rising to the south.
f: A Greek city with a theatre and gymnasium, Ai-Khanoum, stood on the Amu Darya in the 3rd century BC.
The two-humped Bactrian camel is named after this region.
The poet Rumi is known in Persian as Balkhi, 'from Balkh'.

q.q: What was Balkh called in ancient times?

scythian-steppe.name: Scythian steppe
scythian-steppe.t: Grasslands of the nomads and their golden kurgans
scythian-steppe.s: North of the Black Sea stretches the steppe where the Scythians once lived: horse-riding nomads who moved with their herds and buried their leaders under great earth mounds called kurgans. Their goldsmiths made some of the finest animal-style jewellery of the ancient world. Today the land is farmed in huge fields, and from above it looks like a patchwork quilt on a flat table.
scythian-steppe.w: A vast flat plain of large rectangular fields, cut by broad rivers flowing south to the Black Sea.
f: Herodotus devoted a whole book of his Histories to the Scythians.
A gold pectoral found in a kurgan in 1971 is one of the masterpieces of Scythian art.
Kurgans still rise from the fields, some nearly 20 m high.

q.q: Which Greek historian described the Scythians?

colchis.name: Colchis
colchis.t: The land of the Golden Fleece
colchis.s: Between the Caucasus and the Black Sea lies the green, humid lowland of Colchis, in today's western Georgia. Greek myth sent Jason and the Argonauts here to seize the Golden Fleece. Historians note that people in the nearby mountains once caught gold dust from rivers on sheepskins, which may lie behind the legend. From above, look for the flat green plain of the Rioni river opening to the sea.
colchis.w: Look for a flat, very green lowland along the eastern Black Sea, where the Rioni river reaches the coast at Poti.
f: Excavations at Vani have uncovered rich gold jewellery made in Colchis.
The region is one of the wettest in the Caucasus, which keeps it green all year.
Greek colonists founded trading towns on the Colchian coast from the 6th century BC.

q.q: What did Jason seek in Colchis?

urartu.name: Urartu
urartu.t: The Iron Age kingdom of Lake Van and Ararat
urartu.s: Around the vast blue Lake Van lay Urartu, a mountain kingdom of the Iron Age. Its kings built fortresses on rocky crags, cut irrigation canals through the valleys and left inscriptions in cuneiform. Its name survives in Ararat, the snow-capped volcano on its northern edge. From cruise this is superb country: a huge lake, volcano cones and high, bare plateaus.
urartu.w: Look for the huge blue Lake Van, and to its north-east the lone white cone of Mount Ararat.
f: Yerevan grew from the Urartian fortress of Erebuni, founded in 782 BC.
A canal built by King Menua in the 8th century BC still carries water to the Van area.
Lake Van is a salty soda lake where only one kind of fish can live.

q.q: Which city grew from the fortress of Erebuni?

volga-trade-route.name: Volga trade route
volga-trade-route.t: Viking traders on Europe's longest river
volga-trade-route.s: In the Viking Age, traders from Scandinavia rowed their boats down the Volga to the markets of Bulgar and the Caspian, exchanging furs, wax and honey for Arab silver. Some went on to Baghdad. The river still shows the way: follow its wide blue course, now broken by long reservoirs, as it curves south across Russia towards the Caspian.
volga-trade-route.w: Follow the Volga, broad and blue with long reservoirs, curving south towards the Caspian lowlands.
f: Tens of thousands of Arab silver coins have been found in Viking-age hoards in Scandinavia.
In 922 the Arab envoy Ibn Fadlan described meeting Rus traders on the Volga.
The Volga is Europe's longest river, about 3,500 km.

q.q: What coins flowed north along the Volga route?

varangians-to-greeks.name: Route from the Varangians to the Greeks
varangians-to-greeks.t: The river road from the Baltic to Constantinople
varangians-to-greeks.s: Here ran the great river road of early Rus, from the Baltic to Constantinople. Traders and travellers sailed up the Volkhov through Novgorod to Lake Ilmen, dragged their boats overland between rivers, then floated down the Dnieper past Kyiv to the Black Sea. The route helped bind the first East Slavic state together. From above, follow the chain of lakes and the broad Dnieper as it runs south.
varangians-to-greeks.w: Look for Lake Ilmen and the Volkhov in the north, and far to the south the broad Dnieper flowing to the Black Sea.
f: The route is described in the Primary Chronicle, written in Kyiv in the early 12th century.
Where rivers did not connect, boats were hauled overland on rollers along portages.
A 10th-century Byzantine emperor recorded the names of the Dnieper rapids in two languages, Slavic and Norse.

q.q: Which chronicle describes this route?

trans-siberian-railway.name: Trans-Siberian Railway
trans-siberian-railway.t: The longest railway on Earth, Moscow to the Pacific
trans-siberian-railway.s: This is the longest railway line in the world, about 9,300 km from Moscow to Vladivostok. Built between 1891 and 1916, it tied Siberia and the Pacific coast to European Russia and turned a journey of months into one of days. From cruise, look for towns strung along a line through endless taiga, and for its great bridges over the Ob, the Yenisei and the Amur.
trans-siberian-railway.w: Look for a chain of towns and clearings along a line through dark forest, crossing great rivers on long bridges.
f: Construction was formally begun in Vladivostok in May 1891 by the future Tsar Nicholas II.
The line along the southern shore of Lake Baikal has dozens of tunnels cut into the cliffs.
The full journey by train takes about a week and crosses seven time-zone changes.

q.q: Where was construction formally begun in 1891?

chinese-eastern-railway.name: Chinese Eastern Railway
chinese-eastern-railway.s: Instead of following the long Amur bend, Russia built a shortcut straight across Manchuria to Vladivostok between 1897 and 1903. The line crossed the Greater Khingan mountains and the wide Manchurian plain, and at its junction on the Songhua river a new city grew: Harbin. From above, look for the forested Khingan ridges giving way to a vast flat farmland plain.
chinese-eastern-railway.w: Look for forested Greater Khingan ridges in the west, then a vast, flat patchwork of farmland around Harbin.
f: Harbin was founded in 1898 as the railway's hub.
Harbin's old centre still has streets of Russian-style buildings from the railway era.
The line crossed the Greater Khingan through a tunnel about 3 km long.

q.q: Which city grew up as the railway's hub in 1898?

siberian-trakt.name: Great Siberian Road (Siberian Trakt)
siberian-trakt.t: The post road across Siberia before the railway
siberian-trakt.s: Before the railway, this was the road to Siberia. From the 18th century the Siberian Trakt ran from Moscow over the Urals, through Tyumen, Tomsk and Irkutsk to Kyakhta on the Chinese border. Mail coaches, tea caravans and settlers used it, changing horses at post stations. The modern highway and railway follow much of its line through birch forest and taiga, still visible as a thin thread.
siberian-trakt.w: Look for a road and railway threading east through birch forest and taiga, linking towns on the big rivers.
f: Anton Chekhov travelled it in 1890 on his way to Sakhalin and wrote about its mud and its people.
Tea from China came west along the road from Kyakhta.
It was one of the longest roads in the world when it was completed.

q.q: Which writer crossed Siberia on this road in 1890?

great-tea-road.name: Great Tea Road
great-tea-road.t: Tea by camel from China to Russia
great-tea-road.s: For about two centuries, tea from the hills of southern China travelled north by river boat, cart and camel caravan across the Gobi and the Mongolian steppe to the border town of Kyakhta. There it was traded for furs and cloth and carried on across Siberia to Moscow. From above, look for the vast empty Gobi and the green valleys of the Selenga north of Ulaanbaatar.
great-tea-road.w: Look for the pale, empty Gobi giving way to the green Mongolian steppe and river valleys near Ulaanbaatar.
f: A treaty in 1727 made Kyakhta the official place of trade between Russia and China.
Pressed tea bricks were used as money on the steppe.
Kyakhta's merchants became some of the richest people in the Russian Empire.

q.q: Which border town was the hub of the tea trade?

veliky-novgorod.name: Veliky Novgorod
veliky-novgorod.t: A medieval merchant republic that wrote on birch bark
veliky-novgorod.s: On the Volkhov river, just north of Lake Ilmen, stands Novgorod, one of the oldest cities of Russia. For more than three centuries it was a merchant republic whose town assembly, the veche, chose its princes. Its soggy soil preserved over a thousand letters scratched on birch bark by ordinary people. From above, look for the lake and the river flowing north out of it through the city.
veliky-novgorod.w: Look for Lake Ilmen, with the Volkhov river flowing north out of it through the city.
f: The first birch-bark letter was found here in 1951; more turn up every year.
St Sophia Cathedral, built in 1045–1050, is one of the oldest churches in Russia.
Novgorod's monuments became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1992.

q.q: What did archaeologists find in Novgorod in 1951?

staraya-ladoga.name: Staraya Ladoga
staraya-ladoga.t: Where the story of Rus begins
staraya-ladoga.s: Just before the Volkhov river enters Lake Ladoga lies Staraya Ladoga, a village that was once a busy trading town of Scandinavians, Slavs and Finns. Tree-ring dating puts its first buildings in the mid-8th century, making it one of the oldest towns of Rus. Chronicles link it with Rurik, the legendary founder of the first princely dynasty. From above, look for the Volkhov's final stretch and Europe's largest lake.
staraya-ladoga.w: Look for the Volkhov river running north into the south shore of the huge Lake Ladoga.
f: Its earliest timber buildings have been dated by their tree rings to around 753.
Lake Ladoga, just to the north, is the largest lake in Europe.
The stone fortress by the river dates from the 12th and 16th centuries.

q.q: Which lake lies just north of Staraya Ladoga?

kizhi.name: Kizhi Pogost
kizhi.t: Twenty-two wooden domes on a northern island
kizhi.s: On a small island in Lake Onega stands one of the wonders of wooden architecture: the Church of the Transfiguration, built in 1714, with 22 onion domes covered in silvery aspen shingles. Beside it rise a smaller church and a bell tower. Legend says the master builder threw his axe into the lake when he finished. From above, look for Lake Onega's northern bays, scattered with long narrow islands.
kizhi.w: Look for the northern part of Lake Onega, a maze of long, narrow islands and bays in the Karelian forest.
f: The Church of the Transfiguration is about 37 m tall and built entirely of wood.
Its neighbour, the Church of the Intercession, has nine domes.
Kizhi Pogost became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1990.

q.q: How many domes crown the Church of the Transfiguration?

solovki.name: Solovetsky Islands
solovki.t: A fortress monastery on the White Sea
solovki.s: Far out in the White Sea, just below the Arctic Circle, lie the Solovetsky Islands. Monks founded a monastery here in the 15th century, and it grew into a fortress of huge boulders, a trading power and a centre of northern culture. The islands also hold ancient stone labyrinths laid out by earlier peoples. From above, look for a cluster of forested islands dotted with lakes in the open sea.
solovki.w: Look for a cluster of low, forested islands full of small lakes, in the western part of the White Sea.
f: The monastery walls are built of boulders, some weighing several tonnes.
The monks dug canals linking dozens of the island's lakes.
The islands' monuments became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1992.

q.q: Which sea surrounds the Solovetsky Islands?

bolghar.name: Bolghar
bolghar.t: The northern trading capital on the Volga
bolghar.s: Near where the Kama joins the Volga stood Bolghar, capital of Volga Bulgaria and one of the great markets of medieval Eurasia. Furs from the northern forests met silver and silks from the south. In 922 its ruler received an embassy from the Caliph of Baghdad and officially adopted Islam. From above, look for the vast Kuybyshev Reservoir, where two great rivers meet.
bolghar.w: Look for the enormous Kuybyshev Reservoir where the Kama joins the Volga, south of Kazan.
f: The Arab envoy Ibn Fadlan wrote a vivid account of his journey here in 922.
Bolghar became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2014.
The Kuybyshev Reservoir beside it is the largest reservoir in Europe.

q.q: In which year did Volga Bulgaria adopt Islam?

tobolsk.name: Tobolsk
tobolsk.s: Where the Tobol flows into the Irtysh, Russian settlers founded Tobolsk in 1587, and for about two centuries it was the capital of all Siberia. On a high bluff above the rivers stands the only stone kremlin in Siberia, with white walls and church domes. The cartographer Semyon Remezov, who helped build it, also drew the first atlas of Siberia. From above, look for two rivers meeting in the taiga.
tobolsk.w: Look for the meeting of the Tobol and the Irtysh, with the old town on a high bluff above the floodplain.
f: The chemist Dmitri Mendeleev was born in Tobolsk in 1834.
Its kremlin was built of stone around 1700.
Tobolsk was the starting point for many expeditions further east.

q.q: Which scientist was born in Tobolsk?

mangazeya.name: Mangazeya
mangazeya.t: A lost Arctic boomtown of the fur trade
mangazeya.s: In the tundra on the Taz river, above the Arctic Circle, stood Mangazeya, the first Russian town in the Siberian Arctic. For a few decades in the 17th century it boomed on sable furs, reached by sea from the White Sea and by river. Then trade moved away and the town was abandoned. From above, look for the Taz winding through flat, lake-speckled tundra towards the Gulf of Ob.
mangazeya.w: Look for the Taz river winding through flat tundra full of lakes, east of the long Gulf of Ob.
f: Contemporaries called it 'gold-seething Mangazeya' for its riches.
In 1619 the tsar banned the sea route there, fearing foreign ships would follow it.
Excavations have found leather shoes, chess pieces and seals from across Europe.

q.q: What made Mangazeya rich?

gagarin-landing.name: Gagarin's landing site
gagarin-landing.t: Where the first spaceman came back to Earth
gagarin-landing.s: On the morning of 12 April 1961, after one orbit of the Earth, Yuri Gagarin came down by parachute in a field on the Volga steppe, near the city of Engels. As planned, he had ejected from his capsule, which landed separately nearby. The first people he met were a forester's wife and her granddaughter. From above, look for the wide Volga at Saratov, with Engels on its eastern bank.
gagarin-landing.w: Look for the broad Volga at Saratov; the landing site lies in the steppe a little south of Engels on the east bank.
f: Gagarin landed about 108 minutes after launch.
The site is now a memorial park with a tall monument.
Vostok 1 was designed so that the pilot landed apart from the capsule by parachute.

q.q: How did Gagarin land?
q.a: By parachute, apart from the capsule

golden-ring.name: Golden Ring of Russia
golden-ring.t: Old Russian towns of white stone and onion domes
golden-ring.s: North-east of Moscow lies a loop of old towns: Vladimir, Suzdal, Rostov, Yaroslavl, Kostroma and others. Between the 12th and 17th centuries they were princely capitals and monastery centres, and their white-stone churches, kremlins and onion domes still stand among fields and forests. From above, look for the Volga and for round Lake Pleshcheyevo and Lake Nero among the woods.
golden-ring.w: Look for the Volga at Yaroslavl, and smaller round lakes, Pleshcheyevo and Nero, among forest and fields to the south.
f: The name 'Golden Ring' was coined by a journalist in 1967.
The white-stone monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1992.
The Church of the Intercession on the Nerl, from 1165, stands alone in a water meadow.

q.q: When was the name 'Golden Ring' coined?

grand-trunk-road.name: Grand Trunk Road
grand-trunk-road.t: Two thousand years of traffic across the Ganges plain
grand-trunk-road.s: This is one of Asia's oldest and longest roads, crossing the Indo-Gangetic plain from Bengal to Kabul, some 2,500 km. It follows an ancient route, but the 16th-century ruler Sher Shah Suri rebuilt it with rest houses, wells and shade trees. Rudyard Kipling called it a river of life. From cruise, look for the flat green plain with the Ganges and cities strung along the line.
grand-trunk-road.w: Look for the vast flat green plain of northern India, with the Ganges and a line of big cities running north-west.
f: Sher Shah Suri marked distances along it with pillars called kos minars, some still standing.
The road crosses the Khyber Pass on its way to Kabul.
Much of it is still a main highway, now national roads in several countries.

q.q: Which 16th-century ruler rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road?

grand-canal.name: Grand Canal of China
grand-canal.t: The world's longest canal, Beijing to Hangzhou
grand-canal.s: For more than a thousand years this canal carried rice from the fertile south to feed the capital in the north. Begun in pieces as early as the 5th century BC and joined into one system in the early 7th, it runs about 1,800 km from Hangzhou to Beijing, crossing the Yangtze and the Yellow River. In the south it is still busy with barges, and in clear weather its line can be traced.
grand-canal.w: Between Hangzhou and Yangzhou, look for a waterway threading past Suzhou and Wuxi among lakes and fields.
f: It is the longest artificial waterway in the world.
The pound lock, with gates at both ends, was invented in China in the 10th century for canals like this.
The Grand Canal became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2014.

q.q: Which two cities does the Grand Canal link?

great-wall.name: Great Wall of China
great-wall.t: Two thousand years of walls across mountains and desert
great-wall.s: Chinese states and dynasties built walls along their northern frontier for about 2,000 years, and the stone-and-brick wall most people picture was raised by the Ming after 1368. It runs from the Gobi at Jiayuguan to the sea at Shanhaiguan, riding mountain ridges. It is only a few metres wide, so it cannot be seen from cruise height, but the ridges and deserts it crossed are easy to see.
great-wall.w: North of Beijing, look for steep, wrinkled mountain ridges; far to the west, the gravel desert of the Hexi Corridor.
f: A 2012 survey measured all sections built over the centuries at about 21,000 km.
The idea that the wall is visible from the Moon is a myth.
At Old Dragon's Head near Shanhaiguan the wall runs down into the sea.

q.q: How long are all sections of the Great Wall combined?

tea-horse-road.name: Tea Horse Road
tea-horse-road.t: Tea from Yunnan carried over mountains to Tibet
tea-horse-road.s: For more than a thousand years, caravans of mules and porters carried bricks of tea from Yunnan and Sichuan up into Tibet, and brought back horses. The road climbed through some of the deepest gorges on Earth, where the Yangtze, the Mekong and the Salween run side by side, and over passes above 4,000 m. From cruise the land is breathtaking: parallel river canyons and snowy peaks.
tea-horse-road.w: Look for three deep river gorges running side by side from north to south, between ranges of snowy peaks.
f: Tibetans drank tea churned with butter and salt, so demand was constant.
Old market towns such as Lijiang and Shaxi grew up as caravan stops.
Mule caravans still used parts of the route in the mid-20th century.

q.q: What did Tibet trade for Chinese tea?

tokaido.name: Tōkaidō road
tokaido.t: The old coastal highway from Edo to Kyoto
tokaido.s: In the Edo period the Tōkaidō was Japan's busiest road, running about 500 km along the Pacific coast from Edo, today's Tokyo, to the imperial city of Kyoto. Lords, merchants and pilgrims walked it in about two weeks, stopping at 53 post towns. The artist Hiroshige made it famous in a series of prints. Today the bullet train follows almost the same line, with Mount Fuji watching over it.
tokaido.w: Follow the Pacific coast west from Tokyo; Mount Fuji rises just inland, and the route passes the Hakone hills.
f: Hiroshige's print series 'The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō' appeared in the 1830s.
A barrier at Hakone checked travellers' papers on the road.
Parts of the old stone-paved road still survive near Hakone.

q.q: How many post stations were on the Tōkaidō?

kyoto.name: Kyoto, the old imperial capital
kyoto.t: A thousand years as Japan's capital
kyoto.s: From 794 to 1868 Kyoto was the seat of Japan's emperors. Laid out on a grid modelled on the Chinese capital Chang'an, it became the heart of Japanese court culture: temples, gardens, tea ceremony and the tale of Genji. It still holds well over a thousand Buddhist temples and hundreds of Shinto shrines. From above, look for the city filling a flat basin ringed by wooded mountains, with Lake Biwa to the east.
kyoto.w: Look for a city in a flat basin closed by mountains on three sides, with the large Lake Biwa just to the east.
f: When founded in 794, the city was named Heian-kyō, 'capital of peace'.
UNESCO's listing for ancient Kyoto covers 17 temples, shrines and a castle.
Its streets still follow the grid laid out more than 1,200 years ago.

q.q: What was Kyoto called when it was founded in 794?

nara.name: Nara
nara.t: Japan's first permanent capital and its Great Buddha
nara.s: In 710 Japan's court settled in Nara, its first permanent capital, and for most of the 8th century it was the eastern end of the Silk Road. Buddhism flourished, and Emperor Shōmu cast a giant bronze Buddha and housed it in a vast wooden hall at Tōdai-ji. Tame deer still wander its parks. From above, look for a smaller city in a green basin south of Kyoto.
nara.w: Look for a city in a green basin about 40 km south of Kyoto, backed by wooded hills to the east.
f: The Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji, cast in 752, is about 15 m tall.
Its hall is one of the largest wooden buildings in the world.
Nearby Hōryū-ji contains some of the oldest wooden buildings in the world.

q.q: Which animals roam freely in Nara's parks?

gyeongju.name: Gyeongju
gyeongju.s: For almost a thousand years Gyeongju was the capital of the Korean kingdom of Silla, which united most of the peninsula in the 7th century. Its royal tombs are grassy hills right in the city, and nearby stand the temple of Bulguksa and the stone Buddha of Seokguram. Koreans call it a museum without walls. From above, look for a city in a green basin near the east coast.
gyeongju.w: Look for a city in a green basin among hills near Korea's south-east coast, north of Ulsan.
f: Cheomseongdae, a 7th-century stone tower, is one of the oldest surviving observatories in East Asia.
Gold crowns found in its tombs are among Korea's national treasures.
Bulguksa and Seokguram became UNESCO World Heritage sites in 1995.

q.q: Which kingdom had its capital at Gyeongju?

xian-changan.name: Chang'an and the Terracotta Army
xian-changan.t: The start of the Silk Road and an army of clay
xian-changan.s: Today's Xi'an was Chang'an, capital of the Qin, Han and Tang dynasties and the eastern starting point of the Silk Road. Under the Tang it may have been the largest city in the world. Just east lies the tomb of China's first emperor, guarded by thousands of life-size clay soldiers. From above, look for the city's grid on the Wei river plain, with the Qinling mountains rising to the south.
xian-changan.w: Look for a large grid-planned city on the flat Wei river plain, with the Qinling range rising steeply to the south.
f: The Terracotta Army was found in 1974 by farmers digging a well.
Archaeologists estimate there are around 8,000 figures, their faces individually finished.
Xi'an's Ming city wall, about 14 km around, still stands complete.

q.q: Who found the Terracotta Army in 1974?

forbidden-city.name: Forbidden City, Beijing
forbidden-city.s: At the heart of Beijing lies the Forbidden City, the palace of the Ming and Qing emperors from 1420 to 1912. Walled and moated, it holds some 980 buildings under yellow-tiled roofs, and ordinary people could not enter without permission. It sits exactly on the axis that runs through the old city. In clear air its rectangle can be picked out in the middle of Beijing's grid.
forbidden-city.w: In clear weather, look for a large rectangle at the exact centre of Beijing, with a park and hill on its north side.
f: Twenty-four emperors lived here over almost 500 years.
It is the largest surviving palace complex in the world.
Its yellow roof tiles were a colour reserved for the emperor.

q.q: How many emperors lived in the Forbidden City?

anyang-yinxu.name: Yinxu, the Shang capital
anyang-yinxu.t: Where the oldest Chinese writing was found
anyang-yinxu.s: Near today's Anyang on the North China Plain lay the last capital of the Shang dynasty. Its kings asked questions of their ancestors by cracking bones and turtle shells with heat, then carved the questions and answers on them. These oracle bones are the oldest mature Chinese writing, and many of their characters can still be recognised today. From above, look for the flat, intensely farmed plain north of the Yellow River.
anyang-yinxu.w: Look for the flat, densely farmed North China Plain, with the Taihang mountains rising to the west.
f: Oracle bones were identified in 1899, when a scholar noticed writing on 'dragon bones' sold as medicine.
The intact tomb of Fu Hao, a Shang queen and military leader, was found here in 1976.
Yinxu became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2006.

q.q: On what are the oldest Chinese writings from Yinxu?

dunhuang-mogao.name: Mogao Caves, Dunhuang
dunhuang-mogao.t: A thousand years of Buddhist art in the desert
dunhuang-mogao.s: Where the Silk Road entered China from the western deserts lies the oasis of Dunhuang. In a cliff nearby, monks and patrons carved hundreds of cave shrines over a thousand years and covered them with murals and statues. A sealed library cave, opened in 1900, held tens of thousands of manuscripts. From above, look for the green oasis pressed against enormous golden sand dunes.
dunhuang-mogao.w: Look for a small green oasis pressed against a range of huge golden sand dunes, south of the town of Dunhuang.
f: About 490 caves still hold murals and sculptures.
The library cave held the Diamond Sutra of 868, the oldest dated printed book known.
The Mogao Caves became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1987.

q.q: Which dated printed book was found at Mogao?

qufu.name: Qufu, home of Confucius
qufu.t: The hometown of Confucius and his descendants
qufu.s: In this small city on the Shandong plain, Confucius was born in 551 BC. After his death his house became a temple, and over the centuries emperors enlarged it into one of China's grandest complexes. His descendants lived beside it in a family mansion, and are buried in a vast forest cemetery. From above, look for the flat plain south of Mount Tai, the sacred mountain about 70 km to the north.
qufu.w: Look for the flat Shandong plain, with the sacred Mount Tai rising alone about 70 km to the north.
f: The Kong family tree records more than 80 generations of descendants.
The Confucius family cemetery has been in use for over 2,000 years.
Qufu's temple, mansion and cemetery became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1994.

q.q: How many generations does the Kong family tree record?

turpan-jiaohe.name: Turpan oasis: Jiaohe and the karez
turpan-jiaohe.t: An oasis below sea level, watered from underground
turpan-jiaohe.s: The Turpan basin is one of the lowest and hottest places in Asia, yet it is green with vineyards. The secret is the karez: tunnels dug to carry snowmelt from the Tian Shan underground, safe from evaporation. On a narrow island between two rivers stand the ruins of Jiaohe, a Silk Road city carved down into the earth. From above, look for the red Flaming Mountains and the oasis beside them.
turpan-jiaohe.w: Look for a deep desert basin with a long red ridge, the Flaming Mountains, and green oasis fields along it.
f: The lowest point of the basin lies about 150 m below sea level.
Turpan's karez tunnels together run for thousands of kilometres.
Much of Jiaohe was built by digging rooms out of the ground rather than building upward.

q.q: What is a karez?

loulan.name: Loulan
loulan.t: A lost oasis kingdom at the edge of Lop Nur
loulan.s: On the shores of Lop Nur, once a lake at the eastern end of the Tarim basin, stood Loulan, a small kingdom on the Silk Road. When the rivers shifted and the lake shrank, the city was left to the desert, and sand buried its houses and records. From above, look for the vast dry bed of Lop Nur, whose pale concentric rings look like a giant ear.
loulan.w: Look for a huge pale lakebed with concentric rings like an ear, in the desert east of the Taklamakan.
f: The Swedish explorer Sven Hedin found Loulan's ruins in 1900.
Documents found there are written on wood and paper in several languages.
The 'Ear of Lop Nur' rings are shorelines left as the lake dried.

q.q: Which explorer found the ruins of Loulan in 1900?

karakorum.name: Karakorum
karakorum.t: Capital of the Mongol Empire on the open steppe
karakorum.s: In the green Orkhon valley of central Mongolia stood Karakorum, capital of the Mongol Empire in the mid-13th century. Envoys, merchants and craftsmen came from Europe, Persia and China. A European friar who visited in 1254 described a silver tree in the khan's palace that poured out drinks. Little is left today, but the wide Orkhon valley and its rolling steppe are easy to see.
karakorum.w: Look for the broad green Orkhon river valley on open steppe, with forested Khangai mountains to the west.
f: The silver drinking fountain was made by a goldsmith from Paris, Guillaume Boucher.
The Erdene Zuu monastery was built in 1585, partly from the city's ruins.
The Orkhon valley became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2004.

q.q: What fountain stood in Karakorum's palace?

xanadu.name: Xanadu (Shangdu)
xanadu.t: Kublai Khan's summer capital on the grassland
xanadu.s: On the grasslands of Inner Mongolia, Kublai Khan built his summer capital, Shangdu, in 1256. Here the Mongol court hunted and held great feasts, and here Marco Polo described a palace of marble and a bamboo pavilion held by silk cords. Five centuries later a poem turned its name, Xanadu, into a byword for splendour. From above, look for open, rolling grassland dotted with lakes north of Beijing's mountains.
xanadu.w: Look for open, rolling grassland with small lakes and river meanders, about 270 km north of Beijing.
f: Samuel Taylor Coleridge's poem 'Kubla Khan' begins: 'In Xanadu did Kubla Khan a stately pleasure-dome decree'.
The city's layout combined Chinese planning with open space for Mongol tents.
The site of Xanadu became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2012.

q.q: Which poet made Xanadu famous?

taj-mahal-agra.name: Taj Mahal, Agra
taj-mahal-agra.t: A white marble tomb built for love
taj-mahal-agra.s: On a bend of the Yamuna at Agra stands the Taj Mahal, built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Thousands of craftsmen worked for about 20 years in white marble inlaid with coloured stones. Its colour shifts with the light, from pink at dawn to gold at sunset. The tomb is small from cruise height, but the Yamuna's broad curve through Agra is easy to find.
taj-mahal-agra.w: Look for the broad Yamuna curving past the city of Agra, about 180 km south-east of Delhi.
f: The marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan, over 300 km away.
Shah Jahan himself was later buried beside Mumtaz Mahal inside the tomb.
The Taj Mahal became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1983.

q.q: For whom did Shah Jahan build the Taj Mahal?

hampi.name: Hampi (Vijayanagara)
hampi.t: An imperial city among giant boulders
hampi.s: Among piles of giant granite boulders on the Tungabhadra river lie the ruins of Vijayanagara, capital of a great south Indian empire. Around 1500 it was one of the largest and richest cities in the world, visited by Persian and Portuguese travellers who marvelled at its bazaars. After 1565 it was abandoned. From above, look for a strange rocky landscape of boulder hills along the river, near a large reservoir.
hampi.w: Look for rocky boulder-strewn hills along the Tungabhadra river, just downstream of a large reservoir.
f: The stone pillars of the Vittala temple ring with musical notes when tapped.
A stone chariot in the Vittala temple courtyard appears on India's 50-rupee note.
Hampi became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1986.

q.q: What rings when tapped at Hampi's Vittala temple?

mohenjo-daro.name: Mohenjo-daro
mohenjo-daro.t: A planned city with drains, 4,500 years ago
mohenjo-daro.s: On the Indus plain in Sindh stood Mohenjo-daro, one of the largest cities of the Indus civilisation, built about 4,500 years ago. Its streets were laid out in a grid, its houses had bathrooms, and covered brick drains ran beneath the lanes, a level of planning few ancient cities matched. Its writing has still not been deciphered. From above, look for the green ribbon of the Indus winding through dry land.
mohenjo-daro.w: Look for the Indus river's broad green valley winding south through the dry plains of Sindh.
f: Its 'Great Bath', a watertight brick pool, may be the earliest public water tank known.
The city may have been home to around 40,000 people.
Mohenjo-daro became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1980.

q.q: Which famous structure was found at Mohenjo-daro?

bodh-gaya.name: Bodh Gaya
bodh-gaya.s: On the plains of Bihar, beside a slow river, Buddhist tradition holds that Siddhartha Gautama sat beneath a fig tree and became the Buddha. A tree descended from it still grows beside the tall Mahabodhi Temple, and pilgrims come from all over Asia. It is the holiest place in the Buddhist world. From above, look for the flat green Gangetic plain south of Patna, with low rocky hills near the town of Gaya.
bodh-gaya.w: Look for the flat green plain south of Patna, with scattered low rocky hills around the town of Gaya.
f: The Mahabodhi Temple, rebuilt many times, is one of the oldest brick temples in India.
The present tree grew from a cutting linked, by tradition, to the original.
The temple complex became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2002.

q.q: Under what kind of tree did the Buddha find enlightenment?

nalanda.name: Nalanda
nalanda.t: One of the world's first great universities
nalanda.s: For some 700 years, Nalanda was one of the great centres of learning in Asia. Thousands of monks and students lived in its brick monasteries, studying philosophy, medicine, logic and grammar, and its libraries were famous. Students came from China, Korea, Tibet and South-East Asia. The ruins lie in the green plain of Bihar, south-east of Patna, among fields and villages.
nalanda.w: Look for the flat green plain of Bihar, south-east of Patna, with the low Rajgir hills just to the south.
f: The Chinese monk Xuanzang studied at Nalanda in the 7th century.
It is often called one of the world's earliest residential universities.
Its ruins became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2016.

q.q: Which Chinese monk studied at Nalanda?

ajanta-ellora.name: Ajanta and Ellora caves
ajanta-ellora.t: Temples carved straight out of the Deccan rock
ajanta-ellora.s: In the dark volcanic rock of the Deccan plateau, monks and craftsmen cut temples and monasteries straight into cliffs. At Ajanta, Buddhist caves hold paintings up to 2,000 years old. At Ellora, Buddhist, Hindu and Jain shrines stand side by side, including a whole temple carved from a single rock. From above, look for the flat-topped hills and dark soil of the Deccan north of Aurangabad.
ajanta-ellora.w: Look for flat-topped basalt hills and dark farmland north of the city of Aurangabad.
f: Ellora's Kailasa temple was carved from the top down out of one piece of rock.
The Ajanta caves were brought to wide attention in 1819 by a British officer out hunting.
Both sites became UNESCO World Heritage sites in 1983.

q.q: What is special about Ellora's Kailasa temple?
q.a: It is carved from one rock

sigiriya.name: Sigiriya
sigiriya.t: A palace on top of a giant rock
sigiriya.s: From the jungle of central Sri Lanka rises a lone rock about 200 m high. In the 5th century King Kashyapa built a palace on its summit, reached through the paws of a colossal brick lion. Its walls were painted with graceful women, and gardens with pools spread around its base. From above, look for a single dark rock standing out of the green forest, north of Dambulla.
sigiriya.w: Look for a single steep rock rising from flat green forest in the centre of Sri Lanka, near reservoirs.
f: Only the giant paws of the Lion Gate remain.
Visitors scratched poems on the polished Mirror Wall from about the 8th century.
Sigiriya became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1982.

q.q: What remains of Sigiriya's Lion Gate?

lumbini.name: Lumbini
lumbini.s: On the flat Terai plain at the foot of the Himalaya lies Lumbini, where Buddhist tradition says Siddhartha Gautama, the future Buddha, was born. More than two centuries later Emperor Ashoka visited and set up a stone pillar to mark the spot. Today monasteries from many countries surround the sacred garden. From above, look for the flat green plain with the white wall of the Himalaya on the northern horizon.
lumbini.w: Look for the flat green Terai plain in southern Nepal, with the snowy Himalaya on the northern horizon.
f: Ashoka's pillar, from 249 BC, bears an inscription saying the Buddha was born here.
The pillar was rediscovered in 1896.
Lumbini became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1997.

q.q: Who set up the inscribed pillar at Lumbini?

kathmandu-valley.name: Kathmandu Valley
kathmandu-valley.t: Three royal cities in a Himalayan bowl
kathmandu-valley.s: In a green bowl among the foothills of the Himalaya lie three old royal cities, Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur. Their Newar craftsmen filled them with pagoda temples, carved wooden windows and palace squares, and the valley also holds two of the great stupas of Buddhism. From above, look for a round valley filled with city, ringed by green hills, with snow peaks behind.
kathmandu-valley.w: Look for a round valley filled with city and ringed by green hills, with the snowy Himalaya to the north.
f: Legend says the valley was once a lake, drained when the bodhisattva Manjushri cut a gorge.
The white dome of Boudhanath is one of the largest stupas in the world.
Seven groups of monuments in the valley are on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

q.q: According to legend, what was the valley once?

taxila.name: Taxila
taxila.t: Where Greek and Buddhist worlds met in stone
taxila.s: Near today's Islamabad lay Taxila, a crossroads city of the ancient Gandhara region, on routes linking India, Central Asia and Persia. Alexander the Great passed through, and later Buddhist monasteries and a famous seat of learning flourished here. Its sculptors mixed Greek and Indian styles, giving the Buddha one of his earliest human portraits. From above, look for the green hills just north-west of Islamabad.
taxila.w: Look for the green Margalla Hills and the valley just north-west of Islamabad and Rawalpindi.
f: Alexander the Great arrived at Taxila in 326 BC.
Remains of three successive cities have been excavated here.
Taxila became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1980.

q.q: Which art style mixed Greek and Buddhist forms here?

angkor.name: Angkor
angkor.t: Temple-mountains and giant reservoirs of the Khmer
angkor.s: North of the great lake Tonlé Sap lie the ruins of Angkor, capital of the Khmer Empire. Its kings built temple-mountains of stone, and Angkor Wat, from the 12th century, is the largest religious monument in the world. They also dug huge rectangular reservoirs to store the monsoon rains. Those shapes are visible from cruise: look for long straight-edged lakes and moats in the forest.
angkor.w: Look for a long rectangular reservoir and a square moat in the forest, just north of Siem Reap and the Tonlé Sap lake.
f: The West Baray reservoir is about 8 km long and 2 km wide, and still holds water.
The moat around Angkor Wat is about 190 m wide.
The towers of the Bayon temple carry more than 200 giant stone faces.

q.q: Which lake lies just south of Angkor?

bagan.name: Bagan
bagan.t: A plain of more than two thousand temples
bagan.s: On a dry plain beside the Irrawaddy, the kings of Bagan and their subjects built more than 10,000 temples and pagodas between the 11th and 13th centuries. Over 2,000 still stand, brick and white against the ochre earth, turning gold at sunrise. The temples are too small to see from cruise, but look for the wide bend of the Irrawaddy on a flat, dry plain.
bagan.w: Look for a wide bend of the Irrawaddy on a flat, dry ochre plain in central Myanmar.
f: Bagan was the capital of the first kingdom to unite most of Myanmar.
The Ananda temple, from about 1105, is one of its best preserved.
Bagan became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019.

q.q: Roughly how many temples still stand at Bagan?

borobudur.name: Borobudur
borobudur.t: A Buddhist mountain of stone between volcanoes
borobudur.s: On the plain of central Java, ringed by volcanoes, stands Borobudur, the largest Buddhist temple in the world. Built in the 9th century, it rises in terraces like a stepped mountain, and pilgrims walking round it pass thousands of carved panels telling stories of the Buddha. It lay half-buried for centuries. From above, look for the green Kedu plain framed by the volcanoes Merapi, Merbabu and Sumbing.
borobudur.w: Look for a green plain in central Java framed by big volcanic cones, including the often-smoking Merapi.
f: It has 504 Buddha statues and more than 2,600 relief panels.
In 1814 the British governor Stamford Raffles had the overgrown site surveyed.
Borobudur became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1991.

q.q: Who had Borobudur surveyed in 1814?

ayutthaya.name: Ayutthaya
ayutthaya.t: The river-island capital of old Siam
ayutthaya.s: For four centuries Ayutthaya was the capital of Siam and one of the great trading cities of Asia, visited by merchants from Europe, Persia, China and Japan. The city stands on an island where three rivers meet, and its brick temples and prang towers still rise among the modern streets. From above, look for a river-ringed island in the flat rice plain north of Bangkok.
ayutthaya.w: Look for an island ringed by rivers in the flat, watery rice plain about 70 km north of Bangkok.
f: Around 1700 it may have been one of the largest cities in the world.
Foreign traders, including Dutch, Portuguese and Japanese, had their own quarters outside the walls.
Ayutthaya became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1991.

q.q: What makes old Ayutthaya an island?

hoi-an.name: Hội An
hoi-an.t: A lantern-lit trading port frozen in time
hoi-an.s: Near the mouth of the Thu Bồn river on Vietnam's central coast, Hội An was a busy international port where Japanese, Chinese, Portuguese and Dutch merchants traded silk, porcelain and spices. When the river silted up, trade moved to Da Nang, and the old town was left almost untouched, with wooden shophouses, assembly halls and a covered bridge. From above, look for the river mouth and the Cham Islands offshore.
hoi-an.w: Look for the Thu Bồn river reaching the sea about 25 km south of Da Nang, with the small Cham Islands offshore.
f: Its covered bridge was built by Japanese merchants in the late 16th century.
Chinese merchant communities built assembly halls that are still used today.
Hội An's old town became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1999.

q.q: Who built Hội An's covered bridge?

zhongyuan.name: Central Plain, cradle of Chinese civilisation
zhongyuan.t: Where Chinese civilisation took shape on the Yellow River
zhongyuan.s: Along the middle Yellow River lies the Central Plain, where many early Chinese states and dynasties rose. Luoyang and Kaifeng were capitals for centuries, the Shaolin Temple stands on Mount Song, and Bronze Age palaces have been found at Erlitou. From above, look for the broad, silt-brown Yellow River braiding across a vast flat plain, held between high levees.
zhongyuan.w: Look for the wide, muddy Yellow River braiding across a flat plain, with the Song mountains to its south-west.
f: Near Kaifeng the Yellow River's bed lies higher than the surrounding land, held in by levees.
Luoyang's Longmen Grottoes hold tens of thousands of Buddhist statues carved into river cliffs.
Kaifeng, the Northern Song capital, was one of the largest cities in the world around 1100.

q.q: Which temple on Mount Song is famous for kung fu?

ifugao-terraces.name: Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras
ifugao-terraces.t: Mountains sculpted by hand into rice fields
ifugao-terraces.s: In the mountains of northern Luzon, the Ifugao people have carved whole hillsides into steps of rice paddies, fed by water from the forests above. The terraces follow the contours of the slopes like giant staircases, built and maintained by hand over generations. They are too fine to see from cruise, but the steep green Cordillera where they lie is easy to find north of Manila.
ifugao-terraces.w: Look for the steep, green Cordillera range in northern Luzon, about 250 km north of Manila.
f: In 1995 they were among the first sites listed by UNESCO as a living cultural landscape.
The forests above the terraces are kept as shared watersheds to supply the fields.
The Ifugao's Hudhud chants are on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage.

q.q: Which people built the Banaue rice terraces?

trans-saharan-west.name: Trans-Saharan caravan route (Sijilmasa–Timbuktu)
trans-saharan-west.t: Salt south, gold north, across the great desert
trans-saharan-west.s: For centuries camel caravans crossed the western Sahara between Morocco and the Niger. Salt, cloth and horses went south; gold, ivory and leather came north, and the gold of West Africa ended up in coins across the Mediterranean. Books and scholars travelled with them. From above you see the scale of the crossing: weeks of sand seas, gravel plains and bare plateaus with barely a trace of green.
trans-saharan-west.w: Look for endless dunes and gravel plains, dark rocky plateaus, and rare oases strung along dry valleys.
f: The crossing could take around two months, with long stretches between wells.
Mansa Musa of Mali spent so much gold on his pilgrimage in 1324 that its value fell in Cairo.
Salt caravans still carry slabs from the Taoudenni mines to Timbuktu.

q.q: What did caravans carry south to trade for gold?

trans-saharan-bornu.name: Trans-Saharan route: Tripoli–Lake Chad
trans-saharan-bornu.t: The oldest road across the Sahara, via the Fezzan
trans-saharan-bornu.s: From Tripoli, one of the oldest routes across the Sahara ran south through the oases of the Fezzan to Lake Chad and the kingdom of Kanem-Bornu. The Garamantes, who farmed the Fezzan with underground channels, controlled it in Roman times. Later, salt from Bilma and goods from the Mediterranean moved along it. From above, look for dark rocky plateaus, sand seas and, in the far south, the shallow waters of Lake Chad.
trans-saharan-bornu.w: Look for dark plateaus and sand seas in southern Libya, and far south the shallow, marshy basin of Lake Chad.
f: The Garamantes dug long networks of underground water channels, called foggaras.
Kanem-Bornu, at Lake Chad, lasted about a thousand years.
In 1823 British travellers on this route became the first Europeans known to see Lake Chad.

q.q: Which ancient people farmed the Fezzan with underground canals?

vasco-da-gama-route.name: Vasco da Gama's sea route to India
vasco-da-gama-route.t: The voyage that joined Europe to India by sea
vasco-da-gama-route.s: In July 1497 four ships left Lisbon under Vasco da Gama. Instead of hugging the African coast, he swung far out into the South Atlantic, then rounded the Cape of Good Hope, sailed up the east African coast and, with a local pilot from Malindi, crossed the Indian Ocean. In May 1498 he reached Calicut in India. The sea route he opened changed world trade for centuries.
vasco-da-gama-route.w: Look for the Cape Peninsula at Africa's south-western tip, and the long east African coast running north from it.
f: His loop through the South Atlantic kept the fleet out of sight of land for about three months.
He named Natal, in South Africa, after passing it on Christmas Day 1497.
Bartolomeu Dias had first rounded the Cape of Good Hope ten years earlier, in 1488.

q.q: Which region did da Gama name on Christmas Day 1497?

carthage.name: Carthage
carthage.t: The Phoenician city that rivalled Rome
carthage.s: On a headland of the Gulf of Tunis, Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded Carthage, which grew into the great trading power of the western Mediterranean. After Rome destroyed it in 146 BC, the Romans rebuilt it as one of the largest cities of their empire. Its round military harbour can still be traced. From cruise, look for the lagoon-edged Gulf of Tunis and the city of Tunis spread around it.
carthage.w: Look for the Gulf of Tunis and its shallow lagoon, with the capital's suburbs covering the headland to the north-east.
f: Legend says Queen Dido founded the city on land she marked out with strips of an oxhide.
The circular Punic harbour once had sheds for more than 200 warships around its edge.
Carthage became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1979.

q.q: Which legendary queen founded Carthage?

leptis-magna.name: Leptis Magna
leptis-magna.t: A Roman city kept by the sand
leptis-magna.s: On the Libyan coast east of Tripoli lies Leptis Magna, one of the most complete Roman cities in the Mediterranean. It began as a Phoenician port, grew rich on olive oil, and was lavishly rebuilt by Emperor Septimius Severus, who was born here. Later the sand covered it, keeping its forum, basilica, theatre and harbour. From above, look for the coast near Khoms and the dry hills behind it.
leptis-magna.w: Look for the Libyan coastline about 120 km east of Tripoli, near the town of Khoms.
f: Emperor Septimius Severus was born in Leptis Magna in AD 145.
Its theatre faces the sea, and its stage wall still stands tall.
Leptis Magna became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1982.

q.q: Which Roman emperor was born in Leptis Magna?

el-jem.name: El Jem amphitheatre
el-jem.t: A colossal Roman arena in an olive-grove town
el-jem.s: In the middle of the Tunisian plain, a Roman amphitheatre towers over the small town of El Jem. It was built around AD 238 in Thysdrus, a town made rich by olive oil, and could seat some 35,000 people. It is among the best-preserved Roman amphitheatres in the world. The arena is small from cruise height, but the vast plain of olive groves in neat rows is striking.
el-jem.w: Look for a flat plain covered in regular dotted rows of olive trees, inland from the Tunisian coast between Sousse and Sfax.
f: It is one of the largest amphitheatres the Romans ever built.
It was built of stone blocks brought from quarries some 30 km away.
El Jem became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1979.

q.q: Which product made Roman Thysdrus rich?

volubilis.name: Volubilis
volubilis.t: A Roman town at the edge of the Empire in Morocco
volubilis.s: On a fertile plain below the Zerhoun hills lie the ruins of Volubilis, a town at the far south-western edge of the Roman Empire. Its olive presses, triumphal arch and houses with fine floor mosaics still stand among the fields. Centuries later, the founder of Morocco's first Muslim dynasty came here in 788. From above, look for green farmland and hills north of Meknes.
volubilis.w: Look for green farmland and the rounded Zerhoun hills, about 25 km north of Meknes.
f: Dozens of olive presses have been found in the town.
Idris I, founder of the Idrisid dynasty, was received here in 788.
Volubilis became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1997.

q.q: Who founded a dynasty after arriving at Volubilis in 788?

ait-benhaddou.name: Aït Benhaddou
ait-benhaddou.t: An earthen fortress village on the caravan road
ait-benhaddou.s: On a hill above a river south of the High Atlas stands Aït Benhaddou, a fortified village of red earth houses and towers. It guarded the caravan route that brought goods from the Sahara over the mountains to Marrakesh. Its silhouette has starred in many films. From above, look for the snowy High Atlas and the green river valleys on its southern side near Ouarzazate.
ait-benhaddou.w: Look south of the snowy High Atlas for a green river valley and a large reservoir near Ouarzazate.
f: Its buildings are made of rammed earth and mud brick, repaired after heavy rains.
It has appeared in films including 'Lawrence of Arabia' and 'Gladiator'.
Aït Benhaddou became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1987.

q.q: What are Aït Benhaddou's buildings made of?

timbuktu.name: Timbuktu
timbuktu.t: A desert city of scholars and manuscripts
timbuktu.s: Where the Sahara meets the great bend of the Niger stands Timbuktu, a meeting point of camel caravans and river boats. In the 15th and 16th centuries it was a centre of Islamic learning, with mud-brick mosques and scholars whose libraries grew over generations. Europe imagined it as a city of gold. From above, look for the edge where the Niger's green floodplain meets the desert sand.
timbuktu.w: Look for the northern edge of the Niger's bend, where green floodplain and channels give way to desert.
f: Its Djinguereber Mosque dates back to the 14th century and is built of earth.
Families in Timbuktu have kept hundreds of thousands of manuscripts.
In 1828 René Caillié became the first European to reach Timbuktu and return.

q.q: Who was the first European to reach Timbuktu and return?

djenne.name: Djenné
djenne.t: The largest mud-brick building in the world
djenne.s: On an island in the floodplain of the Bani river, in Mali's inland Niger delta, stands Djenné, one of the oldest towns in West Africa. Its Great Mosque is the largest mud-brick building in the world, bristling with wooden beams. Every year the whole town replasters it with fresh mud in a festival. From above, look for a watery maze of channels and floodplain, green or blue in the wet season.
djenne.w: Look for the inland Niger delta, a vast floodplain of channels and lakes, especially after the summer rains.
f: The present Great Mosque was built in 1907 on the site of earlier mosques.
Nearby Djenné-Djeno was a town from around 250 BC, one of the oldest known south of the Sahara.
Old Djenné became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1988.

q.q: What is Djenné's Great Mosque built of?

great-zimbabwe.name: Great Zimbabwe
great-zimbabwe.t: The stone city that gave a country its name
great-zimbabwe.s: In the granite hills of southern Zimbabwe stand the ruins of Great Zimbabwe, capital of a medieval Shona kingdom. Its builders fitted granite blocks into curving walls up to 11 m high without any mortar. Its rulers grew rich trading gold and ivory with the Swahili coast; Chinese porcelain and Persian glass have been found here. From above, look for granite hills and the reservoir of Lake Mutirikwi.
great-zimbabwe.w: Look for rounded granite hills and the large Lake Mutirikwi reservoir near the town of Masvingo.
f: 'Zimbabwe' comes from Shona words usually translated as 'houses of stone'.
Carved soapstone birds from the site appear on Zimbabwe's flag.
Great Zimbabwe became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1986.

q.q: What does the name 'Zimbabwe' mean?

mapungubwe.name: Mapungubwe
mapungubwe.t: The hilltop kingdom of the golden rhino
mapungubwe.s: Where the Limpopo and Shashe rivers meet, at today's meeting point of South Africa, Botswana and Zimbabwe, stood Mapungubwe, the capital of one of southern Africa's first kingdoms. Its rulers lived on a flat-topped sandstone hill above their people and traded gold and ivory towards the Indian Ocean. From above, look for the confluence of two broad, often sandy rivers in dry bush country.
mapungubwe.w: Look for the confluence of the Limpopo and Shashe, two wide sandy rivers, where three countries meet.
f: A small rhinoceros of gold foil over a wooden core was found in a royal grave.
Mapungubwe is seen as a forerunner of Great Zimbabwe.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2003.

q.q: Which golden animal was found at Mapungubwe?

aksum.name: Aksum
aksum.t: Giant stone stelae of an African empire
aksum.s: In the highlands of northern Ethiopia stood Aksum, capital of a trading empire that dealt with Rome, Persia and India and minted its own gold coins. Its kings raised towering carved stone stelae over royal tombs, and in the 4th century King Ezana adopted Christianity. Ethiopian tradition holds that the Ark of the Covenant rests in a chapel here. From above, look for rugged highland plateaus cut by deep valleys.
aksum.w: Look for high, rugged plateaus cut by deep valleys in the far north of Ethiopia.
f: The tallest stela still standing is about 24 m high.
A fallen stela about 33 m long may be the largest single stone ancient people tried to raise.
Aksum became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1980.

q.q: Which king of Aksum adopted Christianity?

lalibela.name: Lalibela
lalibela.t: Churches carved down into solid rock
lalibela.s: High in the mountains of Ethiopia, eleven churches were carved not upward but downward, out of solid volcanic rock, around 800 years ago. King Lalibela is said to have wanted a new Jerusalem, and pilgrims still fill the churches at Christmas. The most famous, St George, is shaped like a cross when seen from above. From cruise, look for rugged highland ridges and deep valleys.
lalibela.w: Look for high, rugged mountains and deep gorges in the Ethiopian highlands, east of Lake Tana.
f: Most of the churches were cut free from the surrounding rock, windows and doors included.
Lalibela was among the first 12 sites on UNESCO's World Heritage list in 1978.
The churches are still used for worship every day.

q.q: What shape is Lalibela's Church of St George?

meroe.name: Meroë
meroe.t: The steep pyramids of the Kush kingdom
meroe.s: On the east bank of the Nile in Sudan, clusters of steep, narrow pyramids rise from the sand. They belong to Meroë, capital of the kingdom of Kush, which once ruled Egypt itself. Its rulers, including powerful queens, were buried under more than 200 pyramids. Meroë also smelted iron on a large scale. From above, look for the Nile's green ribbon, north of Khartoum, in wide desert.
meroe.w: Look for the thin green line of the Nile winding through desert, about 200 km north-east of Khartoum.
f: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt, though they are smaller and steeper.
Kush's ruling queens held the title Kandake, the origin of the name Candace.
Meroitic writing can be read aloud, but the language is still barely understood.

q.q: What title did the ruling queens of Kush hold?

kilwa.name: Kilwa Kisiwani
kilwa.t: The richest of the Swahili city-states
kilwa.s: On a small island off the coast of Tanzania stand the coral-stone ruins of Kilwa, a Swahili city-state that grew rich on the gold trade of the Indian Ocean. Its sultans built a great domed mosque and a vast palace overlooking the sea. The traveller Ibn Battuta visited in 1331 and praised it as one of the most beautiful towns in the world. From above, look for islands, mangroves and turquoise shallows.
kilwa.w: Look for small islands, mangrove channels and turquoise shallows on the coast about 300 km south of Dar es Salaam.
f: The Great Mosque of Kilwa dates back to the 11th century.
Kilwa's coins have been found as far away as northern Australia.
Kilwa became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1981.

q.q: Which traveller praised Kilwa in 1331?

olduvai.name: Olduvai Gorge
olduvai.t: A gorge that opened a window on human origins
olduvai.s: Between the Ngorongoro highlands and the Serengeti plains runs Olduvai Gorge, where layers of ancient lakeside sediment hold nearly two million years of human prehistory. Here Mary and Louis Leakey found early human fossils and some of the oldest stone tools known. From above, look for the vast round Ngorongoro crater and the pale Serengeti plains to its west; the gorge lies between them.
olduvai.w: Look for the huge round Ngorongoro crater; the gorge cuts the plains just north-west of it towards the Serengeti.
f: Mary Leakey found the skull known as 'Nutcracker Man' here in 1959.
Its simple stone tools gave their name to the Oldowan tool-making tradition.
Nearby at Laetoli, footprints about 3.6 million years old were found in volcanic ash.

q.q: Who found the 'Nutcracker Man' skull in 1959?

cradle-of-humankind.name: Cradle of Humankind
cradle-of-humankind.t: Limestone caves full of our ancestors
cradle-of-humankind.s: In the rolling hills north-west of Johannesburg, a cluster of limestone caves has yielded a large share of the world's early human fossils. Famous finds include 'Mrs Ples', a skull more than two million years old, the nearly complete skeleton called 'Little Foot', and a species new to science, Homo naledi. From above, look for the Johannesburg sprawl and the Hartbeespoort reservoir among the ridges to its north-west.
cradle-of-humankind.w: Look north-west of Johannesburg for grassy ridges and the Hartbeespoort Dam reservoir.
f: 'Mrs Ples' was found at Sterkfontein Caves in 1947.
Homo naledi was announced in 2015 from fossils found in the Rising Star cave system.
The Cradle of Humankind became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1999.

q.q: What was the skull found at Sterkfontein in 1947 called?

hadar-lucy.name: Hadar, where Lucy was found
hadar-lucy.t: The badlands where 'Lucy' came to light
hadar-lucy.s: In the hot Afar region of Ethiopia, along the Awash river, eroding badlands expose layers millions of years old. In 1974 a team found here a partial skeleton of an early human relative who lived about 3.2 million years ago. They called her Lucy, and she showed that our ancestors walked upright long before their brains grew large. From above, look for the green Awash valley in dry, volcanic land.
hadar-lucy.w: Look for the green thread of the Awash river winding through dry, dark volcanic land in north-eastern Ethiopia.
f: About 40 percent of Lucy's skeleton was recovered.
In Ethiopia she is also known as Dinkinesh, meaning 'you are marvellous'.
She belongs to the species Australopithecus afarensis, named after the Afar region.

q.q: Which song gave Lucy her name?
q.a: Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds

swahili-coast.name: Swahili coast
swahili-coast.t: Coral-stone towns of the monsoon trade
swahili-coast.s: Along the coast of East Africa grew a chain of trading towns, from Lamu and Mombasa to Zanzibar and Kilwa. Their merchants used the monsoon winds to trade with Arabia, Persia and India, and built in coral stone with carved wooden doors. The Swahili language and culture grew from African roots with many words borrowed from Arabic. From above, look for reefs, lagoons and white beaches along a green coast.
swahili-coast.w: Look for coral reefs, turquoise lagoons and islands along a green coast between southern Somalia and Tanzania.
f: 'Swahili' comes from an Arabic word meaning 'coasts'.
Lamu Old Town is the oldest and best-preserved Swahili town, a UNESCO site since 2001.
Dhows, wooden sailing ships, still use the monsoon winds along this coast.

q.q: What does the Arabic root of 'Swahili' mean?

tassili-rock-art.name: Tassili n'Ajjer rock art
tassili-rock-art.t: Paintings from the time when the Sahara was green
tassili-rock-art.s: On a sandstone plateau in the Algerian Sahara, carved into a maze of rock pillars, are thousands of paintings and engravings. They show giraffes, hippos and elephants, and herders with cattle, in a land that is now desert. The art records how the Sahara changed from green savanna to sand over thousands of years. From above, look for a dark, eroded plateau above the pale dunes near Djanet.
tassili-rock-art.w: Look for a dark, deeply eroded sandstone plateau rising above pale sand seas in south-eastern Algeria.
f: More than 15,000 paintings and engravings have been recorded here.
The plateau's rock pillars are often called a 'forest of stone'.
Tassili n'Ajjer became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1982.

q.q: What do the Tassili paintings reveal about the Sahara?

inca-road.name: Inca road (Qhapaq Ñan)
inca-road.t: An empire tied together by mountain roads
inca-road.s: The Incas built a road network of some 30,000 km along the Andes, from today's Colombia to Chile and Argentina. Its main spine ran through the mountains from Quito to Cusco and on south, with stairways cut into cliffs, rope bridges over gorges and way stations every day's walk. Relay runners carried messages along it. From above, look for high plateaus, snowy volcanoes and Lake Titicaca.
inca-road.w: Look for the high, bare Andean plateau, snowy volcano cones and the big blue Lake Titicaca.
f: The Incas had no wheeled vehicles; the roads served walkers and llama caravans.
The Q'eswachaka rope bridge is still rebuilt by hand every year.
The road system became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2014, shared by six countries.

q.q: Which Inca rope bridge is still rebuilt every year?

camino-real-tierra-adentro.name: Camino Real de Tierra Adentro
camino-real-tierra-adentro.t: The royal silver road from Mexico City to Santa Fe
camino-real-tierra-adentro.s: For almost three centuries this was the main road north from Mexico City, running some 2,500 km through the silver-mining towns of Zacatecas and Durango, across the Chihuahuan desert and up the Rio Grande to Santa Fe. Wagons, mule trains and missionaries moved along it. From above, look for the high desert basins of northern Mexico and the green ribbon of the Rio Grande.
camino-real-tierra-adentro.w: Look for the high, dry basins of northern Mexico, and further north the green line of the Rio Grande.
f: The Mexican part of the road became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2010.
Santa Fe, at its northern end, is the oldest state capital in the United States.
Silver from the mines along it flowed south to Mexico City and on to Spain.

q.q: Which metal drove traffic on the Camino Real?

oregon-trail.name: Oregon Trail
oregon-trail.t: Two thousand miles by covered wagon
oregon-trail.s: In the mid-19th century hundreds of thousands of settlers crossed the continent by covered wagon, on trails to Oregon, California and Utah. The Oregon Trail ran about 3,500 km from Missouri along the Platte River, over the Rockies at South Pass and down the Snake and Columbia rivers. The journey took four to six months. From above, look for the braided Platte River and the high plains of Wyoming.
oregon-trail.w: Look for the wide, braided Platte River across Nebraska, then the high, dry basins of Wyoming.
f: Wagon ruts cut into rock are still visible near Guernsey, Wyoming.
Travellers aimed to reach Independence Rock by 4 July, hence its name.
South Pass let wagons cross the Continental Divide on a gentle slope.

q.q: How did Independence Rock get its name?
q.a: Travellers aimed to reach it by 4 July

route-66.name: Route 66
route-66.t: America's Mother Road, Chicago to the Pacific
route-66.s: Opened in 1926, Route 66 ran about 3,900 km from Chicago to Santa Monica, across prairie, the Texas Panhandle and the south-western deserts. It carried migrants west in the 1930s and holidaymakers in the 1950s, and its motels, diners and neon signs became American icons. Much of it is now replaced by interstates, but from above you can follow its line along the railway across the desert.
route-66.w: Across Arizona and New Mexico, look for a highway and railway running side by side through red desert and mesas.
f: John Steinbeck called it 'the Mother Road' in 'The Grapes of Wrath'.
The 1946 song '(Get Your Kicks on) Route 66' made it famous around the world.
It was officially removed from the US highway system in 1985.

q.q: Which writer called Route 66 'the Mother Road'?

pony-express.name: Pony Express
pony-express.t: Mail at a gallop across the West
pony-express.s: For about 18 months in 1860 and 1861, riders on fast horses carried mail across the American West, from Missouri to California in about ten days. They changed horses at relay stations every few dozen kilometres, across plains, deserts and the Sierra Nevada. Then the telegraph reached California and the service closed. From above, look for the ridges and dry basins of Nevada that the riders crossed.
pony-express.w: Look for Nevada's parallel mountain ridges and dry basins, and the Sierra Nevada rising to the west.
f: The route ran about 3,000 km from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento.
There were around 190 stations along the way.
The service ended two days after the transcontinental telegraph was completed in October 1861.

q.q: What put the Pony Express out of business?

lewis-and-clark.name: Lewis and Clark expedition route
lewis-and-clark.t: Up the Missouri and over the Rockies to the Pacific
lewis-and-clark.s: In 1804 Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out from near St. Louis with the Corps of Discovery to find a route to the Pacific. They paddled up the Missouri, crossed the Rocky Mountains with horses from the Shoshone, and floated down the Columbia to the ocean. Along the way they mapped rivers and described hundreds of plants and animals. From above, follow the Missouri's wide reservoirs across the plains.
lewis-and-clark.w: Look for the Missouri River's long reservoirs across the northern plains, and the Columbia River gorge in the far west.
f: Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman, travelled with them carrying her baby son.
They spent the winter of 1805–06 at Fort Clatsop, near the Pacific coast.
The round trip covered about 13,000 km.

q.q: Which Shoshone woman travelled with Lewis and Clark?

transcontinental-railroad.name: First Transcontinental Railroad
transcontinental-railroad.t: The line that stitched America coast to coast
transcontinental-railroad.s: In the 1860s two companies raced to build a railway across the American West: one east from Sacramento over the Sierra Nevada, the other west from the Missouri River across the plains. They met at Promontory Summit in Utah on 10 May 1869, where a golden spike was driven. A journey that had taken months now took about a week. From above, look for the Great Salt Lake and the high Wyoming basins.
