transcontinental-railroad.w: Look for the Great Salt Lake, with the Promontory peninsula on its north shore, and the dry basins of Wyoming to the east.
f: Chinese workers made up most of the Central Pacific's workforce in the Sierra Nevada.
The news of the golden spike was sent across the country by telegraph as it happened.
The line ran roughly 3,000 km from Council Bluffs to the San Francisco Bay.

q.q: Where was the golden spike driven in 1869?

erie-canal.name: Erie Canal
erie-canal.t: The ditch that made New York the Empire State
erie-canal.s: When it opened in 1825, the Erie Canal linked the Hudson River at Albany with Lake Erie at Buffalo, about 580 km away. Barges could now carry grain and timber from the Great Lakes to New York City far more cheaply than wagons, and the city became America's leading port. Sceptics had called it Clinton's Ditch. From above, look for the Mohawk valley and the chain of Finger Lakes to its west.
erie-canal.w: Look for the Mohawk valley west of Albany, then the long, thin Finger Lakes south of the canal's route.
f: The original canal had 83 locks to climb about 170 m.
At Lockport a staircase of five locks, the 'Flight of Five', lifted boats up a ridge.
It cut the cost of shipping goods from Buffalo to New York by around 90 percent.

q.q: Which lake does the Erie Canal link to the Hudson?

panama-canal.name: Panama Canal
panama-canal.t: A staircase of water between two oceans
panama-canal.s: Opened in 1914, the Panama Canal lets ships cross the isthmus instead of sailing round South America. Locks lift them 26 m into Gatún Lake, a huge reservoir made by damming a river, then lower them to the other ocean. A French attempt had failed; the United States finished the work. From cruise it is easy to see: a lake full of islands, a cut through green hills and ships queueing at both ends.
panama-canal.w: Look for Gatún Lake with its many islands, the narrow cut through hills, and lines of ships waiting off both coasts.
f: Because the isthmus curves, ships going from the Atlantic to the Pacific actually head south-east.
When filled, Gatún Lake was the largest artificial lake in the world.
In 1928 the writer Richard Halliburton swam the canal and paid a toll of 36 cents.

q.q: Which lake forms much of the Panama Canal?

canadian-pacific-railway.name: Canadian Pacific Railway
canadian-pacific-railway.t: The railway that held a new country together
canadian-pacific-railway.s: In 1871 British Columbia agreed to join Canada on one condition: a railway to the Pacific. The Canadian Pacific was finished in 1885, running about 4,600 km from Montreal along the rocky shore of Lake Superior, across the prairies and through the Rockies at Kicking Horse Pass. It carried settlers, wheat and tourists. From above, look for the grid of prairie farms and the wall of the Rockies beyond Calgary.
canadian-pacific-railway.w: Look for the vast grid of prairie fields, then the Rockies rising west of Calgary, with Banff in the valley.
f: The last spike was driven at Craigellachie, British Columbia, on 7 November 1885.
The Spiral Tunnels, opened in 1909, loop inside mountains to ease the steep grade.
The railway built grand hotels, such as the Banff Springs, to attract travellers.

q.q: Where was the Canadian Pacific's last spike driven?

columbus-1492.name: Columbus's first voyage (1492)
columbus-1492.t: The crossing that joined two halves of the world
columbus-1492.s: In August 1492 three small ships left Palos in Spain under Christopher Columbus, stopped in the Canary Islands, then sailed west with the trade winds. After about five weeks at sea they reached an island in the Bahamas on 12 October. Columbus believed he had reached Asia. His voyage began lasting contact between Europe and the Americas, with profound consequences for the peoples of both. From above, look for the turquoise shallows of the Bahamas.
columbus-1492.w: Look for the bright turquoise banks and low islands of the Bahamas, set in deep blue ocean.
f: His ships were the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña.
The route along the north-east trade winds is still used by sailing boats crossing the Atlantic.
The Taíno people called the island where he landed Guanahani.

q.q: What did the Taíno call Columbus's first landfall?

alcock-brown-1919.name: Alcock and Brown, first non-stop transatlantic flight (1919)
alcock-brown-1919.t: The first non-stop flight across the Atlantic
alcock-brown-1919.s: On 14 June 1919 John Alcock and Arthur Whitten Brown took off from a field in St. John's, Newfoundland, in a modified Vickers Vimy biplane. They flew through fog, snow and ice for about 16 hours, navigating by sextant when they glimpsed the sun and stars, and came down in a bog near Clifden, Ireland. It was the first non-stop flight across the Atlantic, and both men walked away unhurt.
alcock-brown-1919.w: At the western end, look for Newfoundland's rugged east coast; at the eastern end, the rocky coast of Connemara.
f: They mistook the bog for a green field, so their plane tipped onto its nose on landing.
They won a £10,000 prize from the Daily Mail and were both knighted.
Their flight covered about 3,000 km.

q.q: Where did Alcock and Brown land?
q.a: In a bog near Clifden, Ireland

lindbergh-1927.name: Lindbergh's New York–Paris flight (1927)
lindbergh-1927.t: Alone across the Atlantic in 33½ hours
lindbergh-1927.s: On 20 May 1927 Charles Lindbergh took off from Long Island in the single-engined Spirit of St. Louis, bound for Paris. He flew alone, fighting sleep, over Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and the open ocean, reached Ireland's coast almost exactly where he had planned, and landed at Le Bourget after about 33½ hours. It was the first solo non-stop flight across the Atlantic, and it made him world-famous overnight.
lindbergh-1927.w: Look for the long coast of Nova Scotia at the American end, and south-west Ireland and Cornwall at the European end.
f: An extra fuel tank blocked his view ahead; he looked forward through a periscope or out of the side windows.
He won the $25,000 Orteig Prize for the first non-stop flight between New York and Paris.
A huge crowd, estimated at over 100,000, met him at Le Bourget.

q.q: How long did Lindbergh's flight take?

transatlantic-telegraph.name: First transatlantic telegraph cable
transatlantic-telegraph.t: The wire that let two continents talk in minutes
transatlantic-telegraph.s: In 1866 the giant steamship Great Eastern laid a telegraph cable along the floor of the Atlantic, from Valentia Island in Ireland to Heart's Content in Newfoundland. News that had taken about ten days by ship now crossed the ocean in minutes. An earlier cable in 1858 had worked only for a few weeks. Today's internet still crosses the ocean by cable, along much the same seabed.
transatlantic-telegraph.w: At the ends, look for the rugged tip of south-west Ireland and the deep bays of eastern Newfoundland.
f: The American businessman Cyrus Field spent twelve years on the project.
The 1858 cable carried a message from Queen Victoria to the US President that took about 16 hours to send.
The Great Eastern was the only ship then big enough to carry the whole cable.

q.q: Which ship laid the 1866 Atlantic cable?

machu-picchu.name: Machu Picchu
machu-picchu.t: An Inca estate on a mountain saddle above the clouds
machu-picchu.s: On a ridge high above the looping Urubamba river, the Inca emperor Pachacuti built a royal estate of granite temples, terraces and houses around 1450. The Spanish never found it, and it drifted out of memory beyond the valley until 1911, when local farmers led the explorer Hiram Bingham there. The site is small from cruise, but look for the deep river gorges and the snowy peaks around it.
machu-picchu.w: Look for the deep, twisting Urubamba gorge north-west of Cusco, with the snowy peak of Salcantay to the south.
f: It lies at about 2,430 m, between the peaks of Machu Picchu and Huayna Picchu.
Its stones were cut to fit so tightly that no mortar was needed.
Machu Picchu became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1983.

q.q: Who brought Machu Picchu to world attention in 1911?

cusco.name: Cusco, the Inca capital
cusco.t: The navel of the Inca world
cusco.s: In a high Andean valley at about 3,400 m lies Cusco, capital of the Inca Empire. Roads ran from it to every corner of the realm, and its temples were covered with gold. After the Spanish arrived they built churches and mansions on the Inca walls, and the fitted stone foundations still line the streets. From above, look for a city filling a green mountain valley, with red-tiled roofs.
cusco.w: Look for a city spread along a high green valley ringed by bare mountains, south-east of the Urubamba valley.
f: Cusco's 'twelve-angled stone' fits its neighbours perfectly without mortar.
Legend says the city was laid out in the shape of a puma.
Cusco became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1983.

q.q: Which animal's shape was Cusco said to follow?

nazca-lines.name: Nazca Lines
nazca-lines.t: Giant drawings scratched into the desert
nazca-lines.s: On the dry plateau of southern Peru, the Nazca people drew hundreds of straight lines, geometric shapes and animal figures by moving the dark surface stones to reveal paler ground. Some are hundreds of metres long, and the dry, windless climate has kept them for 2,000 years. The animal figures need a low-flying plane, but from cruise the longest lines can sometimes be made out as faint pale scratches.
nazca-lines.w: Look for a flat, pale-brown desert plateau between river valleys, inland from the coast of southern Peru.
f: About 70 figures show animals and plants, including a hummingbird, a monkey and a spider.
The German mathematician Maria Reiche studied and protected the lines for about 50 years.
The Nazca Lines became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1994.

q.q: How were the Nazca Lines made?

chan-chan.name: Chan Chan
chan-chan.t: The largest mud-brick city of the Americas
chan-chan.s: On the desert coast of northern Peru stood Chan Chan, capital of the Chimú kingdom. Its walled compounds, built of adobe mud brick and decorated with friezes of fish, birds and waves, covered some 20 km², making it the largest adobe city in the Americas. The Incas conquered it around 1470. From above, look for the green Moche valley meeting the sea beside the city of Trujillo.
chan-chan.w: Look for the green Moche valley reaching the Pacific beside Trujillo, with bare desert on either side.
f: Rain is so rare here that mud walls have survived for centuries.
Each Chimú ruler is thought to have built his own walled palace compound.
Chan Chan became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1986.

q.q: What is Chan Chan built of?

caral.name: Caral
caral.t: A city as old as the Egyptian pyramids
caral.s: In the Supe valley north of Lima stood Caral, one of the oldest cities in the Americas. Around 2600 BC, while the pyramids of Giza were rising, its people built stepped pyramids and sunken circular plazas here, without pottery or writing. They farmed cotton and traded with fishing villages on the coast. From above, look for a thin green valley crossing the coastal desert towards the Pacific.
caral.w: Look for a narrow green valley cutting through the coastal desert, about 180 km north of Lima.
f: The archaeologist Ruth Shady has led excavations at Caral since 1994.
Flutes made of pelican and condor bones were found in one of its temples.
The Sacred City of Caral-Supe became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2009.

q.q: Who has led excavations at Caral since 1994?

tiwanaku.name: Tiwanaku
tiwanaku.t: A high-altitude capital near Lake Titicaca
tiwanaku.s: Near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca, at about 3,850 m, stood Tiwanaku, capital of a civilisation that flourished centuries before the Incas. Its builders shaped stone with astonishing precision and fed the city with raised fields that protected crops from frost. The Incas later saw it as a sacred ancestral place. From above, look for the vast blue lake and the flat, cold altiplano around it.
tiwanaku.w: Look for the southern end of the huge blue Lake Titicaca and the flat high plain stretching away from it.
f: Its Gateway of the Sun was carved from a single block of stone.
Its raised-field farming has been revived in some villages around the lake.
Tiwanaku became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2000.

q.q: What is Tiwanaku's famous carved gateway called?

potosi.name: Potosí and Cerro Rico
potosi.t: A mountain of silver that fed an empire
potosi.s: High on the Bolivian plateau, at about 4,000 m, rises Cerro Rico, the rich hill. After silver was found here in 1545 it became one of the richest sources of silver ever known, largely worked by forced Indigenous labour. The city at its foot grew into one of the largest in the Americas, and its coins spread across the world. From above, look for a reddish cone above a city on the bare high plain.
potosi.w: Look for a reddish, cone-shaped mountain rising above a city on the bare, high Bolivian plateau.
f: The Spanish phrase 'vale un Potosí' still means 'it's worth a fortune'.
Potosí is one of the highest cities in the world.
The city became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1987.

q.q: What does the saying 'vale un Potosí' mean?

teotihuacan.name: Teotihuacan
teotihuacan.t: A city of pyramids that awed even the Aztecs
teotihuacan.s: North-east of today's Mexico City lie the ruins of Teotihuacan, one of the largest cities in the world around AD 500. A broad avenue several kilometres long runs past the great Pyramids of the Sun and the Moon, lined with temples and palaces. Centuries after its fall, the Aztecs believed the gods had been born here. In clear air the Pyramid of the Sun can sometimes be picked out in the valley.
teotihuacan.w: Look north-east of Mexico City's sprawl for a farmed valley with a long straight avenue and two large pyramids.
f: The Pyramid of the Sun is about 65 m tall, one of the largest in the Americas.
At its peak the city may have had around 100,000 inhabitants.
Teotihuacan became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1987.

q.q: What does 'Teotihuacan' mean in Nahuatl?
q.a: Place where the gods were made

tenochtitlan.name: Tenochtitlan
tenochtitlan.t: The Aztec capital built on a lake
tenochtitlan.s: Mexico City stands on the site of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital founded in 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco. Causeways linked it to the shore, canals ran between its districts, and floating gardens fed its people. When Spanish travellers first saw it, they compared it to Venice. The lake was later drained, and from above you now see only a vast city filling the old lakebed, ringed by mountains and volcanoes.
tenochtitlan.w: Look for an immense city filling a high basin ringed by mountains, with the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl to the south-east.
f: The eagle on a cactus on Mexico's flag comes from the city's founding legend.
Remains of the Great Temple were uncovered in the city centre after 1978.
The canals of Xochimilco are a surviving piece of the old lake landscape.

q.q: Which image on Mexico's flag comes from Tenochtitlan's legend?

chichen-itza.name: Chichén Itzá
chichen-itza.t: A Maya calendar in stone on the Yucatán plain
chichen-itza.s: On the flat limestone plain of the Yucatán rises Chichén Itzá, one of the greatest cities of the Maya. Its step pyramid, El Castillo, works as a calendar in stone, and at the spring and autumn equinoxes shadows form a serpent descending its stairs. There are no rivers here; water came from cenotes, natural wells in the rock. From above, look for flat green forest stretching to every horizon.
chichen-itza.w: Look for flat, unbroken green scrub forest across the Yucatán, about 180 km west of Cancún.
f: El Castillo's four stairways plus its top platform add up to 365 steps.
Its Great Ball Court is the largest known in Mesoamerica.
Chichén Itzá became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1988.

q.q: What appears on El Castillo's stairs at the equinoxes?
q.a: A serpent of light and shadow

tulum.name: Tulum
tulum.t: A Maya port on a cliff above the Caribbean
tulum.s: On a low cliff above the turquoise Caribbean stands Tulum, a walled Maya port that was still busy when the first Spanish ships sailed by. Its temples looked out over a gap in the reef, and traders in canoes carried jade, obsidian and salt along the coast. From above, look for the long white-sand coast of the Yucatán and the line of the barrier reef just offshore.
tulum.w: Look for the white-sand coast south of Cancún, with a thin line of surf marking the reef offshore.
f: A stone wall protected the city on three sides; the sea guarded the fourth.
Its name is Maya for 'wall'.
The Mesoamerican Barrier Reef off this coast is the largest reef in the Americas.

q.q: What protected Tulum on three sides?

palenque.name: Palenque
palenque.t: A Maya royal city in the rainforest
palenque.s: Where forested hills meet the lowland plain of Chiapas stands Palenque, a Maya city famous for its elegant temples and carved inscriptions. Its greatest king, Pakal, ruled for almost 70 years in the 7th century. In 1952 archaeologists found his tomb deep inside the Temple of the Inscriptions, with a jade mask and a magnificently carved stone lid. From above, look for green hills rising from the flat plain.
palenque.w: Look where the forested hills of Chiapas rise abruptly from the flat, wet plain of Tabasco to the north.
f: Pakal became king at the age of 12.
The tomb was reached by a hidden stairway inside the pyramid.
Palenque became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1987.

q.q: Whose tomb was found in the Temple of the Inscriptions?

tikal.name: Tikal
tikal.t: Maya temples rising above the jungle canopy
tikal.s: Deep in the rainforest of northern Guatemala, the temple-pyramids of Tikal rise above the treetops. It was one of the most powerful Maya cities, home to tens of thousands of people, with plazas, palaces and reservoirs. Laser scans from aircraft have since revealed thousands more buildings hidden under the forest. From above, look for unbroken green jungle and Lake Petén Itzá to the south.
tikal.w: Look for unbroken green rainforest in northern Guatemala, with the long Lake Petén Itzá to the south.
f: Its tallest temple, Temple IV, is about 65 m high.
Tikal appears as a rebel base in the original 'Star Wars' film of 1977.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1979, for both nature and culture.

q.q: Which film used Tikal as a rebel base?

mesa-verde.name: Mesa Verde
mesa-verde.s: On a green tableland in south-western Colorado, Ancestral Puebloan people farmed for more than 700 years. In the 1200s they built villages of stone into alcoves in the canyon walls, some with more than a hundred rooms. Around 1300 they moved away, probably driven by drought. From above, look for a flat-topped mesa cut by deep canyons, near the Four Corners where four states meet.
mesa-verde.w: Look for a large flat-topped mesa, green with juniper and cut by canyons, in the far south-west of Colorado.
f: Cliff Palace, the largest cliff dwelling, has around 150 rooms.
In 1906 it became the first US national park created to protect human works.
In 1978 it was among the first 12 sites on UNESCO's World Heritage list.

q.q: What is Mesa Verde's largest cliff dwelling?

chaco-canyon.name: Chaco Canyon
chaco-canyon.t: Great houses aligned with the sun and moon
chaco-canyon.s: In a dry canyon in north-western New Mexico, Ancestral Puebloans built great houses of stone, some several storeys high with hundreds of rooms. Chaco was a centre of trade and ceremony, linked to distant settlements by straight roads, and several buildings are aligned with the sun and moon. From above, look for dry mesas and washes in empty desert south of the San Juan River.
chaco-canyon.w: Look for dry mesas, canyons and washes in open desert in north-western New Mexico.
f: Pueblo Bonito, the largest great house, had around 650 rooms.
Chaco is also an International Dark Sky Park, with some of the darkest night skies in the US.
Chaco Culture became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1987.

q.q: What is Chaco Canyon's largest great house?

cahokia.name: Cahokia
cahokia.t: The great city of the Mississippi mound builders
cahokia.s: Just across the Mississippi from St. Louis lie the mounds of Cahokia, the largest city north of Mexico before Europeans arrived. Around 1100, thousands of people lived here among plazas, houses and more than a hundred earthen mounds. Its central mound, built basket by basket, is the largest earthwork of its kind in the Americas. From above, look for where the Missouri and Mississippi rivers meet near the city.
cahokia.w: Look for the confluence of the Missouri and Mississippi just north of St. Louis; the mounds lie on the Illinois side.
f: Monks Mound is about 30 m high and covers some 6 hectares.
A circle of wooden posts, now called Woodhenge, marked sunrise at solstices and equinoxes.
Cahokia became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1982.

q.q: What is Cahokia's largest earthwork called?

kitty-hawk.name: Kitty Hawk: the first powered flight
kitty-hawk.t: Where the Wright brothers first flew
kitty-hawk.s: On the windy sand dunes of the Outer Banks, near Kitty Hawk, Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first controlled, powered flights of an aeroplane on 17 December 1903. The first flight lasted 12 seconds. The brothers, bicycle makers from Ohio, chose the spot for its steady winds and soft sand. Every flight since, including yours, traces back here. From above, look for the long, thin barrier islands off North Carolina.
kitty-hawk.w: Look for a long, narrow chain of sandy barrier islands off North Carolina, with wide sounds behind them.
f: The first flight covered about 37 m, less than the wingspan of many airliners.
Their best flight that day lasted 59 seconds and covered about 260 m.
Neil Armstrong carried a piece of the Wright Flyer's fabric to the Moon in 1969.

q.q: How long did the first powered flight last?

l-anse-aux-meadows.name: L'Anse aux Meadows
l-anse-aux-meadows.t: The Vikings in America, 500 years before Columbus
l-anse-aux-meadows.s: At the northern tip of Newfoundland lie the remains of a Norse settlement from around the year 1000: turf buildings, a smithy and bits of iron and bronze. It is the only confirmed Viking site in the Americas, and it matches the sagas' stories of Leif Erikson reaching a land they called Vinland. From above, look for the northern tip of Newfoundland facing the Strait of Belle Isle, with icebergs in spring.
l-anse-aux-meadows.w: Look for the northern tip of Newfoundland beside the narrow Strait of Belle Isle, often with icebergs in spring.
f: It was found in 1960 by the Norwegian explorers Helge Ingstad and Anne Stine Ingstad.
Tree rings in wood cut by Norse tools show the timber was felled in 1021.
It was among the first 12 sites on UNESCO's World Heritage list in 1978.

q.q: Who found L'Anse aux Meadows in 1960?

signal-hill.name: Signal Hill, St. John's
signal-hill.t: Where the first radio signal crossed the Atlantic
signal-hill.s: On a headland above the harbour of St. John's, Newfoundland, Guglielmo Marconi listened through an earphone on 12 December 1901 and heard three faint clicks sent from Cornwall, about 3,500 km away. It was the first wireless signal across the Atlantic, and it opened the age of radio. His aerial was a wire held up by a kite. From above, look for the narrow harbour entrance of St. John's on Newfoundland's east coast.
signal-hill.w: Look for a narrow gap in the cliffs on Newfoundland's east coast, opening into the harbour of St. John's.
f: The three clicks were the Morse code for the letter S.
Cabot Tower on the hill marks the 400th anniversary of John Cabot's voyage of 1497.
St. John's is the easternmost city in North America.

q.q: Which Morse letter did Marconi hear in 1901?

ellis-island.name: Ellis Island and the Statue of Liberty
ellis-island.t: The gateway for millions of new Americans
ellis-island.s: In New York Harbor, two small islands tell the story of American immigration. The Statue of Liberty, a gift from France, was dedicated in 1886, and from 1892 to 1954 around 12 million immigrants were processed at the station on neighbouring Ellis Island. For many, the statue was their first sight of America. From above, look for the Upper Bay between Manhattan, Brooklyn and New Jersey.
ellis-island.w: Look for the Upper Bay just south-west of Manhattan's tip, with two small islands near the New Jersey shore.
f: The statue's copper skin was designed by Frédéric Bartholdi; Gustave Eiffel designed its iron frame.
Its copper turned green over about 20 years as it weathered.
Ellis Island's main building is now a museum of immigration.

q.q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the US?

kennedy-space-center.name: Kennedy Space Center: the road to the Moon
kennedy-space-center.t: The launch pads that sent people to the Moon
kennedy-space-center.s: On Merritt Island, beside Cape Canaveral on Florida's Atlantic coast, stand the launch pads from which Apollo astronauts left for the Moon. Apollo 11 lifted off from Launch Complex 39A on 16 July 1969, and four days later two people walked on another world for the first time. Space Shuttles and today's rockets launch here too. From above, look for the cape and its lagoons jutting out from the Florida coast.
kennedy-space-center.w: Look for a broad cape and flat island between long lagoons on Florida's Atlantic coast, east of Orlando.
f: The Vehicle Assembly Building, where rockets are stacked, is one of the largest buildings in the world by volume.
Much of the land around the pads is a wildlife refuge.
Launch Complex 39A has sent astronauts to the Moon, Space Shuttles into orbit and modern rockets to the space station.

q.q: Which mission launched here for the first Moon landing?

sutters-mill.name: Sutter's Mill, Coloma
sutters-mill.t: The flake of gold that started the California Gold Rush
sutters-mill.s: In January 1848 a carpenter building a sawmill for John Sutter on the American River noticed flakes of gold in the water. Over the next few years some 300,000 people poured into California, and the small port of San Francisco grew into a city almost overnight. California became a state in 1850. From above, look for the Sierra Nevada foothills and Folsom Lake east of Sacramento.
sutters-mill.w: Look for the oak-covered Sierra Nevada foothills and the Folsom Lake reservoir, east of Sacramento.
f: The carpenter who found the gold was James Marshall.
The gold-seekers of 1849 became known as the 'forty-niners'.
San Francisco grew from about 1,000 people in 1848 to around 25,000 by 1850.

q.q: What were the gold-seekers of 1849 called?

santo-domingo.name: Colonial Santo Domingo
santo-domingo.t: The oldest European city in the Americas
santo-domingo.s: At the mouth of the Ozama river on the south coast of Hispaniola, Bartholomew Columbus founded Santo Domingo in the 1490s. It became the first permanent European city in the Americas, and the first cathedral and hospital in the New World were built here. Its old stone quarter still stands beside the river. From above, look for a large city where a river meets the Caribbean, on the island's southern shore.
santo-domingo.w: Look for a large coastal city on the south shore of Hispaniola, where the Ozama river meets the Caribbean.
f: Its cathedral, finished around 1540, is the oldest in the Americas.
Its streets were laid out on a grid that became a model for Spanish cities in the Americas.
The colonial city became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1990.

q.q: Who founded Santo Domingo?

hohokam-canals.name: Hohokam canals of the Salt River valley
hohokam-canals.s: Long before Phoenix, the Hohokam people turned the Salt River valley green. Over a thousand years they dug hundreds of kilometres of canals by hand, the largest prehistoric irrigation network in North America, and grew corn, beans and cotton in the desert. Some of today's canals follow their routes. From above, look for the vast grid of Phoenix, laced with straight canals, in the Sonoran desert.
hohokam-canals.w: Look for the huge grid of Phoenix in the desert, crossed by long straight canals and ringed by bare mountains.
f: The Hohokam canal network is estimated at more than 500 km.
Phoenix was named in the 1860s for a new town rising on the ruins of an old one.
The Pueblo Grande museum in Phoenix preserves a Hohokam platform mound.

q.q: Why was Phoenix given its name?
q.a: It rose on an ancient town's ruins
x: A rare bird was seen there
It was named after a steamboat

ouro-preto.name: Ouro Preto
ouro-preto.t: A baroque gold-rush town in the Brazilian hills
ouro-preto.s: In the steep hills of Minas Gerais, a gold rush at the end of the 17th century created Ouro Preto, then called Vila Rica. Its gold helped pay for an age of splendour in Portugal, and its miners and merchants filled the town with baroque churches decorated by the sculptor Aleijadinho. From above, look for hilly green country scarred with red earth from mining, south-east of Belo Horizonte.
ouro-preto.w: Look for steep green hills and red-earth mine scars in Minas Gerais, south-east of Belo Horizonte.
f: 'Ouro Preto' means 'black gold', after the dark iron-oxide coating on its gold.
In the 18th century Minas Gerais made Brazil one of the world's leading gold producers.
In 1980 it became Brazil's first UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: Which sculptor decorated Ouro Preto's churches?

hokulea-1976.name: Hōkūleʻa's voyage to Tahiti (1976)
hokulea-1976.t: A canoe that sailed Polynesian history back to life
hokulea-1976.s: In 1976 the double-hulled voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti, over 4,000 km of open ocean, without compass or charts. Its navigator, Mau Piailug from Micronesia, read the stars, swells and birds, as Polynesian navigators had for centuries. The voyage helped show that the settlement of the Pacific was deliberate exploration, not drift. Thousands of people greeted the canoe in Papeete. The ocean it crossed looks endless from above.
hokulea-1976.w: Open ocean between Hawaiʻi and Tahiti; near Tahiti, look for the high green island and the atolls of the Tuamotus.
f: The crossing took about a month.
Mau Piailug learned traditional navigation on the tiny island of Satawal.
Between 2013 and 2017 Hōkūleʻa sailed around the world.

q.q: Who navigated Hōkūleʻa to Tahiti in 1976?

aotearoa-voyage.name: Polynesian voyage to Aotearoa
aotearoa-voyage.t: The last great land on Earth to be settled
aotearoa-voyage.s: Around 1250 to 1300, voyagers from eastern Polynesia sailed south-west across thousands of kilometres of ocean in double-hulled canoes and found a large, cool, forested land: Aotearoa, New Zealand. They navigated by stars, swells and the flight of birds, and carried plants and animals to start new lives. It was the last major land mass on Earth to be settled by people. From above, the scale of that ocean is humbling.
aotearoa-voyage.w: Open ocean south-west of the Cook Islands; at the end, look for the green hills and harbours of New Zealand's North Island.
f: Māori tradition names the homeland of the first voyagers Hawaiki.
Many Māori tribes trace their ancestry to particular voyaging canoes.
The voyagers brought plants such as the kūmara, a sweet potato, with them.

q.q: What is the ancestral homeland called in Māori tradition?

rapa-nui-voyage.name: Polynesian voyage to Rapa Nui
rapa-nui-voyage.t: Across empty ocean to the loneliest island
rapa-nui-voyage.s: Around 800 years ago, Polynesian voyagers sailing east from the islands of Mangareva found a tiny speck of land far out in the Pacific: Rapa Nui, Easter Island. It lies more than 2,000 km from the nearest inhabited island, and finding it on purpose required extraordinary navigation. The settlers went on to carve the famous moai. From above you sense the achievement: nothing but ocean, in every direction.
rapa-nui-voyage.w: Endless open ocean east of Pitcairn; at the end, a small triangular island with three volcanoes.
f: The sweet potato, a South American crop, reached Polynesia before Europeans did.
Genetic studies suggest Polynesians and Native South Americans met around 800 years ago.
Pitcairn, on the way, is now home to fewer than 50 people.

q.q: Which South American crop reached Polynesia before Europeans?

cook-first-voyage.name: James Cook's first voyage (1768–1771)
cook-first-voyage.t: Charting the Pacific in the Endeavour
cook-first-voyage.s: In 1768 James Cook sailed from Plymouth in HMS Endeavour to observe the planet Venus crossing the face of the Sun from Tahiti. He then sailed round both main islands of New Zealand, charting their coasts, and followed the east coast of Australia for the first time by a European ship. The voyage brought back charts, plants and animals unknown to European science. From above, look for New Zealand's long coasts.
cook-first-voyage.w: Look for New Zealand's two long islands and, further west, the east coast of Australia along the Coral Sea.
f: The botanist Joseph Banks collected thousands of plant specimens on the voyage.
The Tahitian navigator Tupaia joined the ship and drew a chart of many Pacific islands.
The Endeavour struck the Great Barrier Reef in 1770 and was repaired at today's Cooktown.

q.q: What did Cook observe in Tahiti in 1769?

overland-telegraph.name: Australian Overland Telegraph Line
overland-telegraph.t: The wire that linked Australia to the world
overland-telegraph.s: In 1872 a single telegraph wire was completed from Adelaide across the heart of the continent to Darwin, where it joined an undersea cable to Java and on to London. News from Europe, which had taken months by ship, now arrived in hours. Repeater stations were built every few hundred kilometres, and one of them grew into Alice Springs. From above, look for red desert and the highway that follows the line.
overland-telegraph.w: Look for red desert crossed by a lone highway and railway, and the long parallel ridges of the MacDonnell Ranges at Alice Springs.
f: The line was about 3,200 km long and needed some 36,000 poles.
The work was led by Charles Todd, South Australia's postmaster and astronomer.
Alice Springs was named after his wife, Alice Todd.

q.q: Who was Alice Springs named after?

kingsford-smith-1928.name: First trans-Pacific flight (1928)
kingsford-smith-1928.t: The first flight across the Pacific, in three hops
kingsford-smith-1928.s: In 1928 Charles Kingsford Smith, Charles Ulm and two American crewmen flew the three-engined Fokker Southern Cross from California to Australia. They stopped in Hawaiʻi and Fiji, and the leg from Hawaiʻi to Suva, over 5,000 km of open ocean, was the longest flight over water yet made. After about 83 hours in the air they landed in Brisbane to a huge welcome. From above, the Pacific they crossed looks endless.
kingsford-smith-1928.w: Open Pacific between Hawaiʻi and Fiji; at the end, the Queensland coast and Brisbane River.
f: The crew flew through storms at night, navigating by stars, compass and drift sight.
The Southern Cross is preserved in a memorial at Brisbane Airport.
The whole journey covered about 11,600 km.

q.q: What was Kingsford Smith's aircraft called?

uluru-kata-tjuta.name: Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa
uluru-kata-tjuta.era: tens of thousands of years – today
uluru-kata-tjuta.t: A living cultural landscape of the Aṉangu
uluru-kata-tjuta.s: In the red heart of Australia rises Uluṟu, a single great sandstone rock, and 25 km to the west the domes of Kata Tjuṯa. For the Aṉangu, the traditional owners, these places are bound up with Tjukurpa, the law and knowledge that shape their lives and land. Their stories are held in the rock's features. From cruise, look for a lone red rock on a flat red plain, and a cluster of domes beside it.
uluru-kata-tjuta.w: A single red monolith rising from a flat red plain, with a cluster of rounded domes about 25 km to its west.
f: The park was handed back to the Aṉangu in 1985 and is jointly managed with them.
At the traditional owners' request, climbing Uluṟu stopped for good in 2019.
UNESCO listed the park for its nature in 1987 and as a cultural landscape in 1994.

q.q: In which year did climbing Uluṟu end?

rapa-nui.name: Rapa Nui (Easter Island)
rapa-nui.t: The moai of the most remote inhabited island
rapa-nui.s: Rapa Nui, Easter Island, is a small triangle of volcanoes in the south-eastern Pacific, more than 2,000 km from the nearest inhabited island. Its people carved hundreds of great stone figures, the moai, most of them from a single volcanic quarry, and stood many on platforms with their backs to the sea. From cruise the island is a small green-brown triangle alone in the ocean, with a volcano at each corner.
rapa-nui.w: A small triangular island in open ocean, with a volcanic crater at each corner.
f: Nearly 900 moai are known on the island.
Most were carved in the quarry of the volcano Rano Raraku.
Rapa Nui National Park became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1995.

q.q: Where were most moai carved?

nan-madol.name: Nan Madol
nan-madol.t: A city of basalt islets on a Pacific reef
nan-madol.s: Off the coast of Pohnpei in Micronesia lie the ruins of Nan Madol, built on about a hundred artificial islets on a coral reef. Its walls are made of long black basalt columns stacked crosswise like logs, some weighing several tonnes. It was the seat of the Saudeleur rulers, who governed the island for centuries. From above, look for a green high island ringed by reef and mangroves.
nan-madol.w: Look for the lush high island of Pohnpei ringed by reef and mangroves; the ruins lie off its eastern shore.
f: Canals between the islets have led people to call it the Venice of the Pacific.
How the builders moved the heavy basalt columns is still debated.
Nan Madol became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2016.

q.q: What are Nan Madol's walls built from?

taputapuatea.name: Taputapuātea marae
taputapuatea.t: The sacred heart of Polynesian voyaging
taputapuatea.s: On the island of Raiatea stands Taputapuātea, a complex of stone ceremonial platforms, or marae, at the centre of the Polynesian world. Navigators set out from here and priests from distant islands came to meet, taking stones from it to found new marae across the Pacific. Its setting of forest, lagoon and a pass through the reef is part of its meaning. From above, look for two islands sharing one lagoon.
taputapuatea.w: Look for two green islands, Raiatea and Tahaʻa, enclosed together in one turquoise lagoon, north-west of Tahiti.
f: Raiatea's ancient name, Havaiʻi, recalls the ancestral homeland of Polynesian traditions.
Voyaging canoes such as Hōkūleʻa have been welcomed here in modern times.
Taputapuātea became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2017.

q.q: What was Raiatea's ancient name?

budj-bim.name: Budj Bim eel traps
budj-bim.t: One of the world's oldest fish farms
budj-bim.s: In the lava fields of south-western Victoria, the Gunditjmara people built channels, weirs and ponds to trap, store and harvest eels. Parts of the system are dated to about 6,600 years ago, making it one of the oldest aquaculture systems known. Stone house foundations stand nearby. From above, look for the volcanic plains and lakes near the coast, with the low cone of Budj Bim.
budj-bim.w: Look for flat volcanic plains, lakes and wetlands inland from Portland, near the low cone of Budj Bim.
f: The lava flow the channels are built in came from the Budj Bim volcano about 30,000 years ago.
The eels were smoked and traded far beyond the area.
Budj Bim became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019.

q.q: What did the Budj Bim channels trap?

lake-mungo.name: Lake Mungo
lake-mungo.t: A dry lake that holds 40,000 years of human story
lake-mungo.s: In the outback of New South Wales lie the dry beds of the Willandra Lakes, full of water in the last Ice Age. On their crescent-shaped dunes, archaeologists found the burials of Mungo Lady and Mungo Man, about 40,000 years old, among the oldest known anywhere, with signs of careful ritual. From cruise the landscape is striking: pale, flat lakebeds with white crescent dunes along their eastern shores.
lake-mungo.w: Look for a chain of pale, dry, flat lakebeds, each with a white crescent-shaped dune on its eastern side.
f: The white crescent dune at Lake Mungo is called the Walls of China.
Mungo Lady is the oldest known ritual cremation in the world.
Mungo Man was returned to his traditional owners at Lake Mungo in 2017.

q.q: What are Lake Mungo's white crescent dunes called?

kakadu-rock-art.name: Kakadu rock art
kakadu-rock-art.era: tens of thousands of years – today
kakadu-rock-art.t: A painted gallery thousands of years deep
kakadu-rock-art.s: Along the sandstone escarpment of Arnhem Land and the rock outcrops of Kakadu, generations of Bininj and Mungguy artists have painted animals, people and ancestral beings, layer upon layer, over thousands of years. Some paintings show the inside of fish and animals, bones and all. The traditional owners still care for the sites. From above, look for a long sandstone cliff line above green wetlands and floodplains.
kakadu-rock-art.w: Look for a long sandstone escarpment above wide green floodplains and winding rivers, east of Darwin.
f: Some paintings show the thylacine, which vanished from mainland Australia thousands of years ago.
Later paintings record the arrival of sailing ships and European visitors.
Kakadu became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1981, for both nature and culture.

q.q: Which style shows animals' bones and organs?

nansen-greenland-1888.name: Nansen's crossing of Greenland (1888)
nansen-greenland-1888.t: The first crossing of the Greenland ice sheet
nansen-greenland-1888.s: In 1888 Fridtjof Nansen and five companions landed on the empty east coast of Greenland and set off on skis across the ice sheet, pulling their sledges. They chose the east so that there would be no turning back. After about six weeks, having climbed to some 2,700 m, they came down to the fjords near Godthåb, today's Nuuk. From cruise the ice sheet looks just as they saw it: white to every horizon.
nansen-greenland-1888.w: Look for the Greenland ice sheet, flat and white to the horizon, with dark mountains and fjords along its coasts.
f: Two of the team, Samuel Balto and Ole Ravna, were Sámi.
They missed the last ship home and spent the winter in Godthåb, living among the Greenlanders.
Nansen later wrote a book about Greenlandic life and customs.

q.q: Why did Nansen cross Greenland from east to west?
q.a: So there was no way back

nansen-fram.name: Nansen's Fram drift (1893–1896)
nansen-fram.t: A ship frozen into the ice on purpose
nansen-fram.s: Nansen believed that sea ice drifted across the Arctic Ocean, so in 1893 he let his specially built ship Fram freeze into the pack north of Siberia and drift with it. With a companion he then left the ship on skis and reached farther north than anyone before. Three years later Fram came free near Svalbard, and every member of the expedition came home. From above, the frozen ocean still looks as it did.
nansen-fram.w: Over the Arctic Ocean, look for white pack ice broken by dark leads of open water, north of Siberia and Svalbard.
f: Fram's rounded hull was designed so that the ice would lift it up instead of crushing it.
Nansen and Hjalmar Johansen reached 86°14′ N in April 1895.
Fram is preserved in its own museum in Oslo.

q.q: How far north did Nansen and Johansen reach?

amundsen-northwest-passage.name: Amundsen's Northwest Passage (1903–1906)
amundsen-northwest-passage.t: The first ship through the Northwest Passage
amundsen-northwest-passage.s: Sailors had long sought a sea route round the top of North America. In 1903 Roald Amundsen set out in Gjøa, a small herring boat, with six men. They spent two winters on King William Island, learning from the Netsilik Inuit how to live on the ice. In 1906 Gjøa reached Nome in Alaska, the first ship to sail through the passage. From above, look for the maze of Arctic islands and channels.
amundsen-northwest-passage.w: Look for the maze of islands and ice-choked channels of the Canadian Arctic, north of the mainland coast.
f: The harbour where they wintered is now the Inuit community of Gjoa Haven.
Amundsen skied about 800 km to a telegraph station in Alaska to send the news home.
Gjøa was only about 21 m long.

q.q: Where did Gjøa spend two winters?

amundsen-south-pole.name: Amundsen's journey to the South Pole (1911)
amundsen-south-pole.t: The first people at the South Pole
amundsen-south-pole.s: In October 1911 Roald Amundsen and four companions set out from their hut on the Ross Ice Shelf with dog sledges. They climbed a great glacier through the Transantarctic Mountains to the polar plateau and reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911, the first people ever to do so. All five returned safely. From above, Antarctica is a blinding white plateau, with mountain ranges breaking through the ice.
amundsen-south-pole.w: A blinding white plateau of ice, with dark peaks of the Transantarctic Mountains breaking through.
f: Their base, Framheim, stood on the Ross Ice Shelf at the Bay of Whales.
They climbed to the plateau up the Axel Heiberg Glacier.
At the Pole they left a tent with a letter for the King of Norway.

q.q: When did Amundsen reach the South Pole?

nordenskiold-vega.name: Nordenskiöld's Vega expedition (1878–1879)
nordenskiold-vega.t: The first ship through the Northeast Passage
nordenskiold-vega.s: In 1878 the Swedish-Finnish explorer Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld sailed the steamship Vega east along the Arctic coast of Siberia. It became the first ship to round Cape Chelyuskin, the northernmost point of Eurasia, and after being frozen in for ten months near the Bering Strait it passed into the Pacific in July 1879. Returning via Suez, Vega was the first ship to sail around Eurasia. From above, look for the Siberian coast and sea ice.
nordenskiold-vega.w: Look for the long, low Arctic coast of Siberia, with sea ice offshore for much of the year.
f: Vega rounded Cape Chelyuskin on 19 August 1878.
While frozen in, the crew got to know their Chukchi neighbours.
Stockholm still celebrates Vega Day on 24 April, the date of the ship's return in 1880.

q.q: Which cape was Vega the first ship to round?

norge-1926.name: Airship Norge over the North Pole (1926)
norge-1926.t: The first undisputed flight over the North Pole
norge-1926.s: In May 1926 the airship Norge left Svalbard with 16 people aboard, among them Roald Amundsen, the American Lincoln Ellsworth and its Italian designer and pilot Umberto Nobile. It crossed the North Pole on 12 May and, after about 70 hours in the air, landed at Teller in Alaska. It was the first undisputed flight over the Pole and the first air crossing of the Arctic Ocean.
norge-1926.w: Over the Arctic Ocean, look for pack ice to every horizon; at the ends, Svalbard's mountains and Alaska's coast.
f: At the Pole the crew dropped the flags of Norway, the United States and Italy.
Its mooring mast still stands at Ny-Ålesund in Svalbard.
Nobile's small dog, Titina, flew with them.

q.q: Who designed and piloted the airship Norge?

chkalov-1937.name: Chkalov's transpolar flight (1937)
chkalov-1937.t: Moscow to America over the top of the world
chkalov-1937.s: In June 1937 Valery Chkalov, Georgy Baidukov and Alexander Belyakov flew a single-engined ANT-25 non-stop from Moscow over the North Pole to North America. After 63 hours, much of it in cloud and icing, they landed at Pearson Field in Vancouver, Washington. It was the first non-stop flight between Europe and America across the pole, pioneering the kind of polar route many flights use today. From above, look for pack ice, then Canada's Arctic.
chkalov-1937.w: Over the Arctic, look for pack ice, then the islands of the Canadian Arctic and the coastal mountains of the Pacific North-West.
f: They had aimed for San Francisco but landed early, short of fuel.
The flight covered roughly 9,000 km.
A monument to the flight stands in Vancouver, Washington.

q.q: Where did Chkalov's crew land in 1937?

beagle-voyage.name: Voyage of the Beagle (1831–1836)
beagle-voyage.t: The voyage that shaped Darwin's big idea
beagle-voyage.s: In December 1831 HMS Beagle sailed from Plymouth to survey the coasts of South America, with a 22-year-old naturalist named Charles Darwin aboard. Over five years he collected fossils, birds and beetles, crossed the Andes on horseback and visited the Galápagos Islands, before the ship returned home round the world. What he saw led him to the theory of evolution by natural selection. From above, look for the long coasts of South America.
beagle-voyage.w: Look for the long Atlantic and Pacific coasts of South America, and the maze of channels at Tierra del Fuego.
f: Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859, 23 years after the voyage ended.
The Beagle Channel at Tierra del Fuego is named after the ship.
Its captain, Robert FitzRoy, later issued some of the first public weather forecasts.

q.q: Who was the captain of HMS Beagle?

magnetic-north-pole-1831.name: North Magnetic Pole, first reached 1831
magnetic-north-pole-1831.t: Where compass needles pointed straight down
magnetic-north-pole-1831.s: On 1 June 1831 the British explorer James Clark Ross reached the North Magnetic Pole on the Boothia Peninsula, in the Canadian Arctic. There the needle of a dip compass pointed straight down. The pole does not stay put: it has wandered more than a thousand kilometres since, across the Arctic Ocean towards Siberia. From above, look for the Boothia Peninsula and the frozen channels around it.
magnetic-north-pole-1831.w: Look for the Boothia Peninsula, the northernmost tip of mainland North America, among frozen straits.
f: Ross was the nephew of the expedition's leader, John Ross.
Amundsen measured the pole's position again from Gjoa Haven in 1904.
The magnetic pole is now much closer to Siberia than to Canada.

q.q: How far has the magnetic pole moved since 1831?
